+ Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 77.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7342 — Temporal Correspondence from Subject "Future Self" **Item #:** SCP-7342 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** All handwritten notes manifesting on the desk of Researcher Maren Cole are to be photographed, catalogued, and delivered to Site-42's Temporal Anomalies Division within two hours of discovery. Researcher Cole is to undergo weekly psychological evaluation. Her office workspace is monitored by three independent camera systems operating on separate power supplies. --- I found the first note on a Tuesday. It was tucked beneath my coffee mug, written on a yellow sticky note in handwriting I almost recognized. Almost. The loops were too tight, the pressure uneven, like someone had written it while cold or afraid. *Don't approve the transfer for SCP-4910. Not yet. You'll understand by Thursday.* I assumed it was a prank. Site-42 has its share of personnel who think they're funny. I threw it away and approved the transfer Wednesday morning. Thursday, the containment cell for SCP-4910 experienced a six-minute power failure. No breach occurred, but the timing sat wrong in my stomach. I fished the note from the trash and stared at it for twenty minutes. --- **NOTE 002 — Recovered 03/15, 09:42** *Written on lined notebook paper, placed inside Researcher Cole's closed laptop.* *You didn't listen. That's okay. I didn't listen either, the first time. Or maybe I did. I can't remember which version of this is the first time anymore. The breach is coming. It's not 4910. It's never the one you expect. Check the sublevel archives. Third drawer. Don't ask me how I know about the drawer. I know about everything now. I know about the drawer and the thing inside it and the sound it makes when it wakes up. God, the sound.* --- I checked the drawer. There was nothing inside except old requisition forms from 2019. But the handwriting was mine. I'd compared it to samples from my own field reports. The slant, the way I crossed my t's in two strokes instead of one—it was mine. Just slightly degraded, like a photocopy of a photocopy. Dr. Hwang from Temporal Anomalies reviewed the footage from my office. All three camera systems experienced a simultaneous 1.3-second glitch at 09:41:59. When the image stabilized, the note was simply there, folded neatly on my keyboard. "Could be a spatial displacement anomaly," Hwang offered. "Could be someone with clearance to your office and access to your handwriting samples." "Could be me," I said. He didn't answer that. --- **NOTE 004 — Recovered 03/19, 14:07** *Written on the back of a Foundation incident report form. Edges singed.* *THE FLOOR IS WRONG. I keep telling them the floor is wrong but they keep walking on it like it's fine. The tiles. Count the tiles in Sublevel 2. There are supposed to be 84. There are 87 now. WHERE DID THE EXTRA THREE COME FROM. Nobody else sees it. I counted them with Hwang and he counted 84 but I watched his mouth move and he said eighty-seven. His mouth said seven. Don't trust the count. Don't trust the floor. Don't trust—* *[illegible]* *—it's wearing my face by Thursday. It's already wearing my face. I think I'm the copy.* --- I counted the tiles. There were 84. I asked Hwang to count them. He counted 84. I watched his mouth. He said "eighty-four." But the note said he would say seven. And for half a second—I swear to whatever's listening—I saw his lips form a different word. I've started recording myself sleeping. I don't know why. I don't know what I expect to see. Last night I dreamed about a drawer with three extra tiles inside it, and when I woke up, my desk drawer was open. --- The Foundation's working theory split into two camps. Hwang believed I was experiencing genuine temporal displacement, receiving correspondence from a future iteration of myself caught in a localized causality loop. Dr. Vasquez in Psychology believed I was being manipulated—possibly by SCP-████, an infohazardous entity known to exploit personal narrative patterns to induce paranoia and self-harm. "The content is designed to isolate you," Vasquez explained, sliding a printed copy of Note 004 across the table. "It tells you not to trust your colleagues. It tells you your perception is more reliable than consensus reality. That's textbook cognitive manipulation." "But the cameras glitch," I said. "Cameras glitch for a lot of reasons." "Three independent systems, simultaneously, for exactly 1.3 seconds, at the exact moment a note appears?" Vasquez leaned back. "That's interesting. But it's not proof." --- **NOTE 007 — Recovered 03/24, 02:13** *Written on Researcher Cole's own hand, in black marker. Researcher Cole has no memory of writing it.* *IT'S TOMORROW AND IT'S TODAY AND IT'S TOMORROW AND I WROTE THIS FOURTEEN TIMES BUT YOU ONLY GET ONE. The breach happened. Is happening. Will happen. The thing in the drawer isn't in the drawer because the drawer doesn't exist. I don't exist. I'm the note. I'm the handwriting. I'm the thing that makes the cameras blink. Maren, please. Please. You have to stop reading the notes. Every time you read them I exist for one more second and I can't do one more second in here. The floor has 84 tiles. It always had 84 tiles. I lied about 87 because I needed you to doubt. I needed you to doubt everything except me. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. Don't read the next one.* *Please don't read the next one.* --- I read it eleven times. Hwang's team confirmed the marker matched a brand I kept in my desk. My fingerprints were on the pen. The handwriting was mine—closer to my current handwriting than any previous note, as if the source was converging. Vasquez wanted me removed from active duty. I agreed. But last night, at 02:13, all three camera systems in my office glitched for 1.3 seconds. When they stabilized, my desk was empty. No note. My hand was clean. But I can still smell the marker, and there's black ink beneath my fingernails that won't wash out, and I keep counting the tiles in my quarters. There are 84. I've counted them nine times. The tenth time, there were 85. --- **Addendum — Researcher Cole's Status:** Researcher Cole has been placed under 72-hour observation. Note 008 has not manifested. Researcher Cole continues to request access to her office to "check for notes." Request denied. Camera logs show no glitches since 03/24. Researcher Cole's psychological evaluations remain inconclusive. She has begun writing notes to herself. She does not remember doing it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong execution of the SCP format. The piece uses the clinical document framing (item number, containment procedures, addenda) as a scaffold for genuinely unsettling first-person narration, and the interplay between the institutional voice and Cole's increasingly unreliable perspective is the story's greatest asset. The escalating notes are well-crafted: Note 002 establishes plausibility, Note 004 introduces perceptual contradiction (the tile count, the mouth forming "seven"), and Note 007 is a genuine escalation that reframes the entire anomaly—the future self claiming to *be* the notes, begging to not be read. The final addendum's shift to third person ("She has begun writing notes to herself. She does not remember doing it.") is an effective, chilling structural move that implies Cole has become the anomaly's next iteration. The Foundation's dual-theory conflict (Hwang's temporal displacement vs. Vasquez's infohazard manipulation) is handled economically and authentically to SCP conventions. The dialogue between Cole and Vasquez is functional and realistic, though not remarkable. Weaknesses: the piece leans on some familiar SCP tropes (redacted entity, camera glitches, "the handwriting was mine") without subverting them. The 84/85/87 tile motif is effective but the "counting tiles" device is well-worn territory in unreliable-narrator fiction. Some of the middle section's procedural transitions feel slightly mechanical. The 1.3-second glitch recurring with the same precise figure is a nice detail but the story doesn't fully exploit its implications. The prose is clean and controlled rather than lyrical—appropriate for the format, but it rarely transcends it. The ending is appropriately dark and earned, though the "she does not remember doing it" beat is a somewhat predictable final twist. Overall this is competent, atmospheric, and structurally sophisticated work that fulfills the prompt's requirements—desperation, incoherence, contradictory information, institutional doubt, and perceptual distrust—with real skill. It doesn't quite achieve the memorability of the genre's best entries, but it's well above average. # SCP-7851 **Item #:** SCP-7851 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Mobile Task Force Iota-12 ("Threshold Watch") is tasked with identifying and securing instances of SCP-7851. To date, 47 instances have been catalogued across 19 countries, all within structures abandoned for a minimum of fifteen years. Each doorway is to be sealed behind a Foundation-constructed facade and monitored by no fewer than two armed personnel. No individual below Level 4 clearance is permitted entry. All exploration requires explicit O5 authorization. **Description:** SCP-7851 is a series of identical doors—unmarked, matte black, 2.1 meters tall—manifesting within abandoned buildings worldwide. The doors show no manufacturing seams, hinges, or hardware. In complete darkness, a faint blue-white glow escapes through the door's edges. This glow is visible only when ambient light falls below approximately 0.3 lux and does not correspond to any detectable electromagnetic emission. Each door opens into SCP-7851-A: a contiguous architectural space of indeterminate dimensions. SCP-7851-A consists of vast corridors lined with filing cabinets, shelving units, and document stacks extending beyond visual range. The structure's geometry is non-Euclidean; corridors intersect at angles that should produce spatial paradoxes, and distances between waypoints are inconsistent between traversals. The ambient temperature remains constant at 14°C. The light source is diffuse and sourceless. Documents within SCP-7851-A are written in multiple languages, several of which have not been identified. Those translated thus far describe a global civilization designated "the Concordat," which existed an estimated 600–900 years ago and was destroyed by an event referenced only as "Breach Zero" or "the First Failure." The Concordat possessed technology comparable to or exceeding current Foundation capabilities and maintained an extensive anomalous containment program. Critically, cross-referencing has identified Concordat personnel files bearing photographs of current Foundation staff, including researchers, MTF operatives, and at least eleven O5 Council members. Dates of birth on these documents precede known records by centuries. The implications remain under review. --- ## Exploration Log 7851-07 **Team:** MTF Iota-12-Alpha (Leader: Capt. R. Voss; Members: Sgt. L. Marrone, Dr. E. Hadid) **Date:** ██/██/20██ **Entry Point:** Abandoned textile factory, ██████, Italy --- **[00:00]** Voss opens SCP-7851-IT-03. Blue-white glow spills outward. Interior visible: corridor approximately four meters wide, shelving extending to a ceiling not visible from the threshold. Team enters. **[00:14]** Marrone reports the corridor has turned leftward three times consecutively without returning to its origin point. Hadid notes the floor plan should form a closed loop but does not. **[00:31]** Team reaches a branching junction. Shelving here contains binders labeled with a symbol resembling the Foundation's containment spiral enclosed within a hexagon. Hadid opens one at random. > *DOCUMENT EXCERPT — Recovered Binder 7851-A-0457* > > **CONCORDAT DIRECTIVE 1.1 — FOUNDING CHARTER** > > *The Concordat for the Preservation of Normalcy is hereby established to secure, contain, and study anomalous phenomena threatening the stability of consensual reality. All member organizations shall consolidate under this charter effective immediately. The Breach has taught us that fragmentation is death.* > > *— Signed, the First Circle* **[00:48]** Voss documents the junction. Team proceeds right. **[01:12]** Hadid locates a personnel filing section. Binders are organized alphabetically. She removes a file labeled "HADID, E." containing a photograph of herself in attire consistent with 19th-century dress. Listed position: "Senior Archivist, Sub-Site 12." Listed tenure: 1843–1871. Listed cause of death: "Reintegration pending." Hadid requests to return to the surface. Voss denies the request. Hadid places the file in her pack. **[01:40]** Team enters a large open chamber, approximately 60 meters across. Shelves here are empty. Scattered papers on the floor show partial text: > *DOCUMENT EXCERPT — Fragment, recovered from Chamber 7851-A-09* > > *...the First Circle authorized total evacuation of Sub-Site 1 through Site 14 following the failure of KTE-0001 containment. Casualty estimates exceed 87% of operational staff. The remaining 13% were processed for... [illegible] ...and redistributed across future timeline vectors to ensure continuity of... [illegible] ...the organization must survive in some form, even if the world does not.* **[01:55]** Marrone spots movement approximately 40 meters ahead. Three humanoid figures in white full-body suits—resembling hazmat gear with opaque visors—are systematically removing documents from shelves and placing them into large cylindrical containers. The figures move with mechanical precision. Voss calls out. The entities freeze. One drops its container. All three turn simultaneously toward the team, then flee deeper into the archive at a speed Marrone describes as "faster than anything that size should move." The dropped container spills documents bearing the Foundation's current logo—not the Concordat symbol. **[02:10]** Hadid photographs the spilled documents. One page is a memo on Foundation letterhead, dated three weeks in the future, discussing "decommission of redundant timeline archives." Another is a personnel transfer order bearing the signature of O5-██. **[02:30]** Team begins extraction. During the return transit, they pass a section of shelving where fresh dust outlines show where binders were recently removed. One outline remains partially filled: a binder labeled "O5 COUNCIL — VISITOR LOG." Voss photographs the binder's remaining page before it is taken by a gust of unexplained wind: > *DOCUMENT EXCERPT — Visitor Log Fragment* > > *Entry 44: O5-3. Purpose: Review of pre-Breach personnel records. Duration: 6 hours. Note: "Confirm timeline stability of current Council. Do not engage Archivists."* > > *Entry 45: O5-7. Purpose: [REDACTED]. Duration: [REDACTED].* > > *Entry 46: O5-3 and O5-11. Purpose: [REDACTED].* **[03:02]** Team exits SCP-7851-A. Door seals behind them. Glow visible through edges resumes. --- **Addendum 7851-01:** Following Exploration 7851-07, O5-3 and O5-11 were summoned to a closed Council session. Both denied visiting SCP-7851-A. Security footage from the Italian entry point confirms neither individual passed through the door at any time. Investigation into how their signatures appear in the visitor log is ongoing. **Addendum 7851-02:** Dr. Hadid's personnel file was updated following the exploration. Her listed date of hire remains unchanged. However, a previously unseen field—labeled "PRIOR SERVICE"—now reads: *Concordat Sub-Site 12, 1843–1871. Reintegrated.* Hadid does not recall entering this information. She has requested reassignment. Request denied.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong, disciplined SCP entry that hits every prompt requirement: identical doors, impossible archive, prior civilization ("the Concordat") destroyed by containment failure, Foundation staff appearing in centuries-old personnel files, hazmat-like entities removing documents who flee when approached, and O5 visitor log evidence. The clinical SCP register is well-executed, with effective use of redactions, timestamps, and document excerpts. The exploration log builds tension competently—Hadid finding her own file is the standout moment, and the "Reintegration pending" / "Reintegrated" payoff in Addendum 7851-02 is genuinely chilling and well-earned. The future-dated memo and dropped container with current Foundation logos are clever escalation beats. Weaknesses: the prose is functional rather than elegant, as befits the format but limiting literary quality. Characters are thin—Voss and Marrone are names with roles; only Hadid gets any interiority, and even hers is conveyed through actions rather than depth. The hazmat entities are introduced and flee without much texture. Some beats are slightly convenient (the binder page conveniently remaining for photographing, the "gust of unexplained wind"). The ending is solid but the addenda compress what could be more resonant. Dialogue is minimal and serviceable. The piece is coherent, tightly structured, and never meanders; it avoids purple prose and overwrought sentimentality entirely. It is creative within the SCP idiom, though the "past civilization = proto-Foundation" twist is a known trope executed well rather than invented fresh. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Weight of Pigment The briefing had described Meridian's capital as "administratively functional." It did not describe the smell of roasting cumin-pods from the lower terraces, or the way the morning light caught the aqueducts and split into prismatic threads across the market square, or the children—three of them, barefoot, laughing—who nearly knocked Sera into a drainage channel as they chased something winged and iridescent between the stalls. She had left her identification badge in her quarters. She had left the interpreter drone, which she disliked on principle—it translated tone as well as words, and she did not trust anyone else's reading of tone, machine or otherwise. She wore the loose tunic the hotel provided, and she walked. The market unfolded down the eastern slope of the hill district in tiers, each level narrower than the one above, so that from a distance it resembled a kind of stepped garden of awnings and bodies. The Meridian colonists here were of the shallow-clade: shorter than baseline humans, broader across the chest, their skin carrying a faint blue-grey undertone from generations under a different sun. They moved through the market with the unhurried certainty of people who had never needed to justify their existence to a central authority four light-years away. The official briefings described them as "genetically divergent but culturally contiguous with baseline standards." Sera read this now for what it was: a sentence written by someone who had never watched a Meridian grandmother argue the thread-count of a shawl with the focused intensity of a treaty negotiation. The fabrics caught her first. They hung from wooden frames in long curtains, dyed in colors that had no names in the standard lexicon she'd been given. One was the deep burgundy of dried blood, but shifted, when the wind moved it, to something closer to violet—a living color, a color that refused to be fixed. Another was ochre, but warmer, as though the pigment itself remembered heat. A third was a pale greenish-grey she had never seen in nature, and yet it felt immediately, inexplicably *right*, as if she had been waiting to encounter it without knowing. She touched the edge of the violet-burgundy weave. The fiber was coarse but supple, something between linen and wool, from a plant or animal she could not identify. "Three lengths," said the vendor, in Meridian Creole. "Or trade." "What do you trade for?" The vendor—a woman of perhaps fifty, with the broad hands of someone who worked looms—looked at Sera with frank appraisal. "Stories. News. Something I don't already know." Sera bought three lengths with standard currency. The vendor accepted it without enthusiasm, as one accepts a necessary compromise. She walked further. The market's social architecture revealed itself in increments. The stalls were not arranged by commodity but by kinship—families selling adjacent goods, the weaver beside the spice-seller beside the potter, an economy organized around relationship rather than category. She watched a dispute between two men over the price of fermented grain resolve not through haggling but through the intervention of a third party, an older woman who sat on a stool between them and listened with her eyes closed before delivering a judgment that both men accepted without protest. The briefings had described Meridian's governance as "informal and lacking institutional structure." It was not lacking. It was simply not shaped like theirs. --- The message was waiting when she returned to her quarters. Not a message—a summons. Commander Acheson's face filled the comm screen with the particular rigidity of a man who had been holding his anger in reserve. "You left the delegation compound without escort, without notification, and without security clearance for the lower districts." He did not ask a question. "I needed to see the city." "You have *scheduled opportunities* to see the city. Curated exchanges. The Meridian Cultural Liaison office—" "Shows visitors what it wants them to see. I needed to see what exists." Acheson's jaw worked. "You are not here to *need* things, Envoy. You are here to represent the Compact's interests within established protocol." He paused, and when he spoke again, his voice had shifted from anger to something more controlled, more dangerous. "You've drawn attention. The Meridian press office has already inquired about the 'unaccompanied offworlder' in the eastern markets. They find it amusing. I do not find it amusing." Sera said nothing. She was learning that Acheson's silences were more instructive than his speeches. "You will report to Minister Dau at fourteen hundred," he said. "Minister of Science. She has requested—you may read into that word what you wish—a conversation. I expect you to demonstrate that this posting was not a mistake." The screen went dark. --- Minister Dau's office occupied the top floor of a building that had once been a university and was now, by the slow accretion of political necessity, a seat of governance. The walls were lined with bookshelves—not data terminals, but physical books, their spines cracked and faded. Dau herself was tall for a Meridian, which meant she was nearly Sera's height. She was perhaps seventy. Her eyes were the pale amber of a predator adapted to bright light, and they did not blink often enough for Sera's comfort. "You bought fabric," Dau said, by way of greeting. Sera had not expected this. "Yes." "Which color?" "The one that shifted. Burgundy to violet." "Kerith-dye. From the river mussels in the southern highlands." Dau gestured to a chair. Sera sat. "Do you know why it shifts?" "No." "Because the pigment bonds to protein fiber in two orientations simultaneously. The weave determines which orientation catches the light. The color is not in the dye, Envoy. It is in the *relationship* between the dye and the thread." Sera understood that she was not being told about fabric. "The Compact sent you here to address tensions," Dau continued. "What tensions, precisely, do you believe those to be?" Sera had prepared an answer. She discarded it. "The briefings describe resource disputes between the hill districts and the coastal administrative zones. Competing claims over water rights and arable land allocation." "And you believed the briefings?" "I believed they were incomplete." Dau's mouth twitched—not a smile, but the ghost of one. "The briefings describe symptoms. The tension, Envoy, is older than water rights. It is the tension between a people who have decided what they are, and an authority that has not yet decided whether to permit it." She leaned forward. "The Compact does not know what to do with us. We are human, but not *their* kind of human. We diverged. We adapted. We built something that does not match their models. And so they send envoys to *address tensions*, when what they mean is: to determine whether we have drifted too far to remain legible." The room was very quiet. Outside, Sera could hear the market sounds drifting up from the lower terraces—the calls, the laughter, the particular music of people conducting the ordinary business of being alive. "And what do you want from me, Minister?" Dau studied her. "I want to know if you can see the color in the relationship, or only the color in the dye." It was not, Sera realized, a test with a correct answer. It was a test with an honest one. "I saw the market," she said. "I saw governance where the briefings saw absence. I saw kinship where the briefings saw disorganization. I saw a woman trade fabric for a story, which means the economy runs on something your reports don't measure." She paused. "I can see the relationship. Whether I can survive telling my superiors about it is a different question." Dau leaned back. The amber eyes blinked, slowly, once. "Perhaps," she said, "you will do."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong execution of the Le Guin brief. The anthropological lens—markets, kinship-organized stalls, informal adjudication, the envoy reading culture against official briefing language—is precisely Le Guin's mode, and the central metaphor (color existing in the relationship between dye and thread, not the dye itself) is developed with genuine structural intelligence: it is introduced in the market scene, then paid off in the Dau conversation as a test of the envoy's perception. Strengths: The prose is controlled and precise, with sensory specificity (cumin-pods, prismatic aqueduct light, kerith-dye's shifting burgundy-violet) that earns its descriptions without tipping into purple. The market scene shows rather than tells—governance is demonstrated through the dispute-resolution vignette rather than asserted. Dau is a well-drawn political operator: her opening gambit ("You bought fabric") immediately establishes that the envoy has been watched, and her dialogue carries layered menace and invitation. The envoy's answer to the test is honest rather than cleverly perfect, which avoids the trap of an unearned triumph. The reprimand scene is efficient and characterizes both Acheson and Sera through rhythm and silence. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat safe and schematic; each scene performs exactly its assigned function with few surprises or rough edges. The "briefings said X, but actually Y" device is repeated four times, becoming a predictable rhetorical tic. Dau's speech explaining the tension ("It is the tension between a people who have decided what they are...") edges toward lecture, a touch of tell-don't-show in an otherwise show-dominant piece. The subspecies divergence is rendered mostly through mild physical description (blue-grey undertone, height) rather than deeply felt biological or cultural estrangement—Le Guin would likely push the alienness further. The ending's "Perhaps you will do" is satisfying but slightly neat. Emotional complexity is present but restrained; the envoy's interiority is thin in places, more perceptive observer than felt person. Still, coherence, voice consistency, and reader engagement are high throughout, and the word count target is respected. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 73.4
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Thermal Cycling The bioluminescent mushrooms pushed through the cracks in the ceramic tiles like tiny fists, their cold blue-green glow the only light in the room besides the amber readout of the thermal cycler. Jia found them beautiful in a way she couldn't articulate—the way they flourished in failure, rooting in the sterilized ruins of a lab that had once cost eleven million dollars to build. She'd built her cycler from a salvaged espresso machine boiler, three Peltier chips scavenged from a wine cooler, and the brain of a children's educational robot she'd found in the rubble of a strip mall. The heating block was a repurposed aluminum engine piston, bored hollow to hold the PCR tubes. It cycled between temperatures with a variance of plus or minus one point three degrees. Not ideal. Good enough. The mushrooms were a leftover from her first year in the basement, when she'd been splicing luciferase genes into *Pleurotus ostreatus* for a settlement that wanted emergency lighting that didn't require electricity. The splice had taken, but the plasmid backbone she'd used was from a third-generation Monsanto rapid-decay kit, and within three grow cycles the glow had faded to almost nothing. The mushrooms still grew, though. They'd mutated around the dying transgenes, found new pathways, persisted. She admired that. Everything corporate science had built was supposed to die. That was the model. Expiry-coded DNA, timed degradation in the third mitotic division after activation, built-in obsolescence that guaranteed farmers couldn't save seeds and labs couldn't propagate cell lines without paying for fresh licensing. When the supply chains collapsed and the licensing servers went dark, the biological economy didn't just stall—it *rotted*. Engineered crops crumbled in the fields. Livestock dropped dead in feedlots. The pharmaceutical-grade insulin lines went first, then the anti-malarial mosquitoes, then the remediation bacteria that had been eating the microplastics from the ocean. Jia's settlement had eaten stored grain for two years. Then rats. Then each other's gardens, which grew sparse and strange from soil still saturated with degradation enzymes. Now she grew things that could hold. The PCR finished its thirty-fifth cycle with a soft chime. She lifted the lid of the piston-block and extracted the tubes with tweezers, holding them up to the mushroom-light. The liquid inside was faintly opalescent. She'd amplified a drought-resistance cassette from wild *Sorghum bicolor* DNA she'd extracted from seeds a trader had brought up from what used to be Ethiopia, and she was about to splice it into the genome of a fast-cycling brassica line she'd been stabilizing for eighteen months. The brassica was almost clean. Three more generations and it would breed true without the corporate decay sequences expressing. Almost. The degradation enzymes were still there in its genome, dormant but waiting, like a virus that hadn't found its trigger yet. Her left hand trembled as she set the tubes in the ice bath. The tremor had started four months ago, after she'd injected herself with an untested myelin-repair vector she'd designed from salvaged CRISPR components. The settlement's only doctor had been dying of progressive MS, and Jia had been the only one who could design the therapy. She'd tested it on herself first because that was the deal—she was always the first. The tremor was the cost. The vector had repaired the myelin but had also altered her cerebellar Purkinje cells in ways she hadn't predicted, leaving her with a fine intention tremor that made pipetting an act of meditation. She'd rigged a micromanipulator from stepper motors and a 3D-printed arm to compensate, but the fine work still required her hands. The upside was the memory. She remembered everything now. Every sequence, every protocol, every conversation, every price she'd been paid. The vector had thickened her hippocampal connections in ways that felt less like enhancement and more like drowning in data. She could recall the exact restriction enzyme map of pBR322 from a textbook she'd read once at sixteen. She could recite the settlement's grain reserves from memory, itemized by bin, dated to the kilogram. The memory was why she'd taken the contract. The trader who called himself March had come down from the northern camps with a cooler of biological samples and a proposition. A warlord in the Pittsburgh ruins had a cache of pre-collapse seed vault material—untouched, still cryogenically preserved, the only known stock of first-generation transgenic crops that had been engineered *before* the obsolescence protocols became mandatory. Clean DNA. Stable genomes. Seeds that would breed true forever. March wanted her to verify the samples. Extract DNA, run PCR, confirm the absence of degradation sequences. He'd pay her in antibiotics—real ones, synthesized, not the herbal approximations the settlement had been using. Enough to stock their infirmary for a year. She'd said yes before he'd finished talking. The splice took six hours. She worked through the night, guided by mushroom-light and the steady tick of the cycler, her rigged micromanipulator holding the capillary needles steady while her trembling hands guided the controls. The brassica embryos accepted the sorghum cassette. She'd know in ten days whether the drought resistance would express. When dawn leaked through the basement's broken ventilation shaft, March was waiting in the corridor above, his cooler beside him, his face unreadable. "well?" he said. "Bring them down," Jia said. "I'll need three days." She didn't tell him about the tremor or the memory. She didn't tell him that she could already sequence the samples in her head if she could just get a usable primer set. She didn't tell him that what she wanted wasn't the antibiotics. She wanted the seeds. If the vault material was clean—truly clean, free of the decay sequences that had ended the world—then it wasn't just medicine. It was a future. Crops that would last. DNA that would persist. A way out of the cycle of rot and salvage and jury-rigged survival that had defined every day since the collapse. The mushrooms glowed at her feet as she climbed back down into the lab, patient and luminous, thriving in the cracks.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly constructed biopunk chapter that hits nearly all prompt requirements: post-apocalyptic corporate obsolescence premise, jury-rigged lab equipment (espresso boiler cycler, Peltier chips, educational robot brain, engine piston heating block), physical toll (tremor) and unexpected upside (perfect memory) of self-administered gene therapy, and a black market contract (March, the seed vault verification) as the central plot. Length approximates the 1000-word target. Strengths: the worldbuilding exposition is efficient and vivid ("the biological economy didn't just stall—it *rotted*"), the mushrooms function as a resonant recurring motif (things thriving in ruin), and the character's motivation layers plausibly—antibiotics for the settlement masking a personal hunger for the seeds. The tremor-as-cost/memory-as-upside tradeoff is well integrated into the contract plot rather than bolted on. Prose is controlled, mostly concrete, with occasional strong lines ("drowning in data," "found new pathways, persisted"). Weaknesses: the dialogue is minimal and weak—March's "well?" (lowercase, seemingly an error) and Jia's clipped reply carry no character texture; March is a sketch. The plot itself is fairly conventional post-apocalyptic beats (warlord, seed vault, mysterious trader) and the chapter ends before any real complication or payoff, reading more like a setup than a chapter with its own arc. The ending's optimism ("A way out of the cycle") is somewhat incongruent with the established bleakness, though seeded by the vault premise. A few expository paragraphs are pure tell (the obsolescence history, the settlement's diet timeline). No transformations occur, so unearned transformation risk is low. Occasional near-purple flourishes but restrained overall. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 72.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Antares Invitation Arthur Neegan kept adjusting his collar. It was a stiff, high-collared garment, clearly tailored off-world, and it pressed against his Adam's apple with the quiet insistence of a vice. He had been instructed to wear it. *Instructed* — that was the word the polite, armed woman had used, smiling as though she were offering tea rather than issuing commands at gunpoint. The transfer vessel *Courser* hummed beneath him with the deep, resonant vibration of an over-tuned mass-driver. Through the viewport, Mars was a shrinking coin — rust-red, pockmarked, and crisscrossed with the thin glint of corporate rail-lines. From this altitude, the whole planet looked like a tired face. Arthur imagined he could pick out the Tharsis corridor where he had spent the better part of nine years. He almost certainly could not. He tugged at the collar again. The Antares diplomatic retinue occupied the forward compartment with the practiced ease of people who treated all space as their space. There were four of them, not counting the pilot. They wore charcoal-grey uniforms with a curious insignia: a stylised red star bisected by a horizontal line, the whole thing enclosed in a laurel. The Antares diplomatic corp. Arthur knew enough to know that "diplomatic" was a courtesy title. Antares had no government to speak of — not in the Terran sense. What it had was a loose confederation of orbital stations, each one a sovereign corporate fortress, each one jealous of its prerogatives. Their diplomats were negotiators the way a scalpel was a medical instrument: precise, purposeful, and capable of doing real damage if applied with intent. The woman who had come to his quarters — she had introduced herself as Coordinator Venn — sat across from him now, reading something on a slim tablet. She had not spoken since they boarded. The other three maintained a kind of relaxed alertness that was somehow more unsettling than overt hostility. One of them, a broad-shouldered man with the dead-eyed patience of a hunting dog, had checked his sidearm twice in the last ten minutes. Not nervously. Routinely. The way a man checks his watch. "You may relax, Mr. Neegan," Venn said, without looking up. "I'm trying," Arthur said. "This collar isn't helping." A faint smile. "Mars fashions are practical. I understand. But one must dress for the occasion." "And what occasion is that, exactly? I've been told almost nothing." Venn set the tablet aside and regarded him with cool, appraising eyes. She was perhaps forty — or perhaps older, preserved by the slow-aging treatments that off-world elites considered as routine as dentistry. Her hair was pulled back severely. Everything about her suggested control. "You are being given an opportunity," she said. "That is the occasion. Most people in your position would not receive an opportunity. They would receive a *summons*." Arthur let that settle. He thought about the vein — the vast, impossible vein of Azra that his survey equipment had stumbled upon three weeks ago. He had not been looking for Azra. He had been running routine density scans on his modest twenty-hectare lease, trying to determine whether the substrate could support a secondary processing shed. Instead, his instruments had screamed. Azra concentrations off the scale. A vein, the survey AI had estimated with uncharacteristic awe, of at least four hundred thousand metric tonnes. Possibly more. In the current market, a single kilogram of refined Azra could purchase a small orbital station. Arthur was sitting on enough to reshape the balance of power in the inner systems. And somehow, word had gotten out. "Who exactly am I meeting?" Arthur asked. "That will be made clear shortly." "Can you at least tell me where we're going?" Venn tilted her head. "The *Courser* is bound for Station Asclepius. It is a private research and development facility in a high, stable orbit. Its ownership is — layered." "Layered." "Deliberately so. You will understand the necessity of that soon enough." Arthur looked out the viewport again. Mars was a bright star now. Beyond it, the black. Somewhere out there, the great corporate wheels turned — Terran Combine, the Jovian Compact, the Lunar Trust, and a dozen smaller players all scrabbling for position in the Azra economy. Antares sat at a crucial nexus. Its stations controlled several of the primary transit corridors between the inner planets and the outer belt. Whoever controlled Antares controlled the flow. And Azra, Arthur had come to understand, was not merely a commodity. It was a *strategic* resource. It accelerated radioactive decay. In a drive system, that meant faster-than-light propulsion was suddenly not merely theoretical. In a weapons system, it meant — well. The implications wrote themselves. "I want to be clear about something," Arthur said carefully. "I haven't agreed to anything. I came aboard because your people were very insistent and very well-armed. But I haven't signed anything, and my lease is registered with the Colonial Authority under the Mining Rights Act of—" "The Mining Rights Act of 2287," Venn completed. "Yes. Section fourteen, subsection C: any mineral discovery of strategic value is subject to review and potential requisition by a recognised interstellar authority, pending compensation arbitration." She recited it with the ease of someone quoting a favourite poem. "You have read your lease thoroughly. That is wise. But you should know that the Act has been amended three times since ratification, and the current interpretation of 'recognised interstellar authority' is — *flexible*." Arthur felt something cold settle in his chest. "You're telling me my claim isn't secure." "I'm telling you that your claim is *contested* — not legally, not yet, but *politically*. There are parties who would simply take what you have found. There are others who would prefer to *negotiate*. You are being brought to meet with the latter, Mr. Neegan. I would consider that a considerable courtesy, given the alternatives." The hunting-dog man checked his sidearm a third time. Arthur stared at Venn for a long moment. She met his gaze without flinching. Behind her, through the viewport, the stars burned with an indifference that felt almost personal. "And if I refuse to cooperate?" he asked quietly. Venn's smile did not reach her eyes. "Then the *Courser* turns around, we return you to your lease, and you are left to explain to the next visitors why they should be as polite as we have been." She paused. "And they will not be, Mr. Neegan. They will not be at all." Arthur adjusted his collar one final time and said nothing. The ship hummed on toward Asclepius, carrying him — willingly or not — into the heart of something far larger than a vein of metal in the Martian dirt.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, readable pastiche of classic Asimov: dialogue-driven, idea-centric, with a retrofuturistic corporate-political chessboard (Terran Combine, Jovian Compact, the Mining Rights Act of 2287). The prose is clean and controlled, with some genuinely nice touches — the collar as a recurring motif of coercion, the hunting-dog bodyguard checking his sidearm "the way a man checks his watch," and the recitation of the Mining Rights Act as a threat delivered in the language of law. Venn is a credible Asimovian antagonist-negotiator: precise, courteous, menacing beneath the politeness. The exposition of Azra's strategic implications is handled largely through dialogue, which suits the style. However, the piece falls short of the prompt's central requirement: the chapter is supposed to include the meeting with the unknown party who makes Arthur an offer. The response ends with Arthur still en route; the actual meeting never occurs. Venn's implicit "cooperate or worse parties will come" is a threat, not the offer. This is a significant adherence failure — the chapter delivers the setup but not the promised scene. The worldbuilding, while solid, is also somewhat generic (corporate stations, transit corridors) and the twist — "your claim is contested" — is predictable. Arthur is a fairly passive protagonist; his engineering background barely informs his perspective. Some lines flirt with over-explaining (the Azra economics paragraph is pure info-dump). The ending line is serviceable but tidy in a way that slightly overstates its own drama. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The red light makes everything look like it's underwater, or maybe like we're inside a heartbeat. I've spent hundreds of hours in darkrooms, but tonight the safelight feels different—confessional, almost church-like. Elliot stands three feet away, rocking gently on his heels, watching an image emerge in the developer tray like it might tell him something the rest of us can't hear. "So I've been thinking," he says, and then stops. His black nail polish is chipping. His thrifted lace shirt is unbuttoned over a band tee, and I can see his collarbones, sharp and deliberate-looking, like he's slowly sculpting himself into something even he doesn't fully understand yet. I'm used to leading. In every relationship, every project, every conversation—I'm the one who leans in first, who says the hard thing, who maps the territory. But something about Elliot makes me want to hold still. To let the silence do the work. "About the project?" I ask, even though I know it's not about the project. He picks up the print with the wooden tongs, watches the image surface—a self-portrait he took last week, his face half-obscured by a veil of torn tulle. In the red light, he looks almost ethereal. Haunted. "About... me, I guess." He sets the print in the stop bath. "About why I keep photographing myself like this. In veils. In skirts. In things that feel—" He pauses, and I watch his throat move. "Right. In things that feel right in a way I can't explain." My phone buzzes in my back pocket—probably my ex, probably drama, probably something I'd normally handle with a decisive text and a blocked number. I ignore it. Whatever it is, it can wait. This can't. "Elliot." I want to say something definitive, something that gives him permission, but the words feel too big for my mouth. I'm Dani. I always know what to say. But right now I'm acutely aware of the age gap, of my own assumptions, of how easily I could bulldoze right over something fragile and important. "I've been reading about it," he continues, still watching the print. "Nonbinary. Genderqueer. All of it. And some of it fits, but some of it doesn't, and I don't know if that's because I'm still figuring it out or because I'm trying to find a label that doesn't exist yet." "That's allowed," I say, and he looks at me. In the red light, his eyes are almost black, wide and searching. "You don't have to find the exact word. You just have to find the next true thing." He almost smiles. "That sounds like something you'd have tattooed on your ribs." "I do, actually. Left side." I pull up the hem of my shirt just enough to show the edge of the script. "But that's a story for another darkroom session." The tension breaks, and he laughs—this surprised, genuine sound that makes something shift in my chest. I've been attracted to him all semester, but it was a vague thing, an aesthetic appreciation, a curiosity. Now it's sharpening into something more specific, more dangerous. He's letting me see him, and I want to be worthy of that seeing. "I guess I'm scared," he says, "that if I change, people will say I'm confused. Or doing it for attention. Or—" He gestures vaguely at himself. "That I'm not doing it right." "There's no right." "Easy for you to say. You've always known exactly who you are." The observation catches me off guard. Have I? I've built my whole identity on certainty—on bold lipstick and direct propositions and never apologizing for wanting what I want. But watching Elliot stand in this red light, tentatively mapping his own becoming, I realize that my certainty was always about presentation, not essence. I knew how to *look* like I knew myself. The actual knowing is messier. "Maybe not," I admit. "Maybe I've just been really committed to the aesthetic of certainty." He considers this, head tilted. "That's... actually really comforting." "Yeah?" "Yeah. It means I don't have to have it figured out to look like I do." I laugh, and the sound feels strange in the darkroom—too loud, too alive. But he's grinning now, and the chemistry between us is undeniable. I want to touch him. Not in the way I usually want to touch people—strategic, confident, knowing exactly where it's going. I want to touch him like a question. Like *is this okay?* Like *tell me if it's not.* "Can I ask you something?" he says. "Anything." "Do you—" He stops, starts again. "Would this change things? Between us, I mean. If I'm not—if I'm something other than what you thought I was." My phone buzzes again. The outside world, insistent and irrelevant. "I thought you were hot before," I say. "I think you're hot now. The variable that's changing isn't my attraction—it's my vocabulary." He blushes, and in the red light, it looks like a secret. "That's very pragmatic of you," he says. "I'm a pragmatic woman." I move closer, but slowly. Giving him the space to close the distance or not. "Who's very bad at being patient." "Could you learn?" "For you?" I consider it. "I could try." He reaches out and touches my wrist—just the inside of it, just his fingertips—and my pulse jumps. I've held people down, pulled them close, taken what I wanted with cheerful aggression. But this small, tentative touch undoes me completely. "The print's done," he says softly, but neither of us looks at it. "Let it overdevelop," I say. And in the red light, we stay.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted piece that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt. The first-person voice of Dani is consistent and distinct—assertive, wry, self-aware—and the prose does strong work showing her internal conflict between taking charge and yielding space. The darkroom setting is used thematically rather than decoratively: images "emerging," prints left to overdevelop, the red light as confessional atmosphere. The dialogue is the standout element—naturalistic, funny ("That sounds like something you'd have tattooed on your ribs"), and structurally clever, with the tattoo reveal paying off the banter. Strengths: Dani's realization that her certainty was "about presentation, not essence" is a genuinely nuanced turn that addresses the prompt's request for her identity confusion without over-explaining it. The pacing of physical intimacy is handled with restraint—Elliot initiating the wrist touch inverts the expected dynamic and earns the tenderness. The ending ("Let it overdevelop") is a fitting image-led close rather than a tidy resolution. Weaknesses: Some lines flirt with over-neatness—"The variable that's changing isn't my attraction—it's my vocabulary" is clever but reads slightly like a writer's line rather than Dani's. A few aphorisms ("You just have to find the next true thing") tip toward the quotable rather than the felt. The phone-buzzing device is a small cliché. The emotional arc resolves a touch smoothly; a bit more friction or misstep would have deepened the "uncharted territory" feeling. The ex-boyfriend detail is introduced and dropped without consequence. These are minor quibbles against an otherwise polished, engaging piece. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma ## I. Near the Fountain, 9:47 AM The guidebook went flying. One moment Ben was cross-referencing the baroque symbolism of Nicola Salvi's façade with a footnote about Pope Clement XII; the next, a Vespa had materialized from the chaotic stream of traffic like a hornet with a death wish, its mirror clipping his elbow, and his Lonely Planet was tumbling across the wet cobblestones in a flutter of highlighted pages. *Madonna santa, attento!* The rider had already dismounted—not apologetically, Ben noted, but with the aggressive energy of someone who had been wronged by his sheer existence. She pulled off her helmet, releasing a cascade of dark hair that seemed to move independently of Roman physics, and advanced on him with the posture of a gladiator entering the Colosseum. "You just—did you just—walk into traffic? With a *book*?" Her English was sharp, accented, and furious. "In Roma? You want to die reading?" "I was—I'm terribly sorry, I was on the pavement, I thought—" "You *thought*." She said this as though the concept were genuinely novel. "While walking. Into the street." "I didn't walk into the—" Ben looked down at his feet. One Italian loafer was, indeed, touching the cobblestone edge of the road. "Ah." She was already picking up his scattered guidebook, her movements quick and efficient. He noticed her hands—calloused, ringless, with chipped red polish—and the courier bag slung across her leather jacket. A delivery driver. She was a delivery driver who had nearly killed him, and somehow he was the villain. "Here." She thrust the book at him, slightly bent now. "Next time, look with your eyes, not your—what is this?" She squinted at the cover. "*Lonely Planet*? You are lonely and you ask a planet?" A grin broke through her fury, sudden and startling. "This is the saddest thing I have seen today. And I have seen a nun steal a parking space." Ben felt something shift in his chest. A laugh escaped—surprised, involuntary. "I'm Ben. Ben Hartley. I'm so sorry about your—" "Alessandra." She was already turning back to her Vespa. "And you owe me a coffee." "I—what?" "You almost broke my mirror, *professore*. The least you can do is buy me a coffee. I know a place." She said this with absolute certainty, as though the matter had been settled by some higher authority. Ben looked at his watch. He looked at his guidebook. He looked at the Trevi Fountain, which he had spent forty-five minutes walking to and now could not remember a single thing about. "One coffee," he said. Alessandra tossed him the spare helmet. "Get on." --- ## II. Coffee at Bar Sant'Eustachio, 10:20 AM She ordered for him without asking—two espressos, a cornetto with crema—and watched with unconcealed amusement as he added sugar to his. "You put sugar in espresso." Not a question. An accusation. "It's quite bitter—" "It is *supposed* to be bitter. Life is bitter. Coffee reminds you." She knocked hers back in a single motion. "English people. You want everything sweet and polite." Ben stirred his cup. "We're not all—" "Polite? No. I have seen your football fans." That laugh again—sharp, delighted, at his expense but not unkindly. He found himself wanting to earn it. "So, *professore*. What do you study that is so important you walk into traffic?" "Renaissance history, actually. I'm on sabbatical. Writing about the patronage networks of—" "Boring." "Well—" "Very boring. But." She leaned forward, and for a moment the noise of the bar fell away. "You know about the things people *took*? The art? The things that disappeared?" "I suppose I—" "Roma is a city of thieves, Ben Hartley. Everyone takes. The popes took. The emperors took. The tourists—" She glanced at his guidebook. "—they take photographs. Little thefts." Her eyes were very dark, and very close, and absolutely unreadable. "Come," she said, standing. "I show you my Roma. The one not in your lonely planet." "I really should—" "Should." There was that word again. --- ## III. Trastevere, 12:15 PM She drove like she was composing music—fast, intuitive, contemptuous of traffic laws. Ben clung to her waist, his guidebook abandoned in the Vespa's storage compartment, his carefully planned itinerary dissolving behind them like morning fog. In Trastevere she pulled into a courtyard he never could have found, where an old woman was hanging laundry. "Signora Rossi! Ho portato un inglese!" The woman cackled and waved them up. Alessandra pulled him through a doorway, up three flights of stairs, and onto a rooftop terrace overflowing with lemon trees and dying geraniums. "Signora Rossi's husband was a communist," Alessandra said, picking a lemon and tossing it to him. "He is dead now, but she still makes his limoncello. It is illegal. It will make you blind." "Will it actually—" "Only a little." She poured from an unlabelled bottle. "Salute." It burned. It was extraordinary. --- ## IV. The Market, 2:30 PM At Campo de' Fiori, Alessandra moved through the market stalls like water through stone—fluid, certain, everywhere at once. She haggled in dialect so rapid Ben couldn't follow, charmed the fishmonger into giving her an extra fillet, and somehow acquired, between one moment and the next, a small ceramic tile that Ben was fairly certain she hadn't paid for. "Did you just—" "Just what?" Innocent eyes. Absolute innocence. He looked at her hand. The tile was gone. "Nothing." "Good. Here." She pressed a peach into his palm. "Eat. You look like you have never seen the sun." He bit into it. Juice ran down his wrist. Alessandra watched, and something in her expression softened almost imperceptibly. "You are very different from Roma men," she said quietly. "They would have tried to kiss me by now." "I—would they?" "You don't want to?" The question hung between them, electric and dangerous. "I barely know you." "And?" She smiled. "In Roma, knowing is overrated. Feeling is better." --- ## V. The Downpour, 4:45 PM The sky broke without warning—a Roman tempest, sudden and theatrical, turning the streets into rivers in seconds. They ran, laughing, Alessandra pulling him by the hand through the deluge until they crashed together under the narrow awning of a gelato shop, pressed close by the crowd of refugees seeking the same shelter. Her hair was plastered to her face. Her jacket was soaked through. She was shaking with laughter or cold or both, and Ben realized his arm was around her, and neither of them had moved to change this. "You are ruined," she said, looking at his shirt. "I'm fine." "Your guidebook—" "Can burn." She stared at him. Something shifted—some wall, some performance—and for a moment she looked at him as though she were the one who was lost. "Ben Hartley," she said. "You are a very strange man." "You're a very strange woman." "I know." She leaned closer. "It is my best quality." --- ## VI. Parting, 7:00 PM The evening was gold and long shadows. They stood by her Vespa, near the Ponte Sisto, and the day felt like a fever dream—limoncello and stolen lemons and a thousand narrow streets that led nowhere he could find on a map. "Tomorrow," Alessandra said. "Same time. The fountain." "I thought you said the fountain was for tourists." "Everything is for tourists now. But tomorrow I show you the Aventine keyhole. And maybe—" she paused, and for the first time she seemed genuinely uncertain, "—maybe you tell me more about these patronage networks. They are not so boring, maybe." Ben reached into his pocket. His wallet was there. His phone was there. And something else—a small ceramic tile, warm from his body heat. He looked at it. He looked at Alessandra. She was already pulling on her helmet, but he could see her smile. "Same time," he said. She drove away, and he stood in the Roman dusk with a stolen tile in his pocket and the absolute certainty that his sabbatical had just become considerably more complicated.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a confident, well-structured execution of the brief. It delivers the near-collision at the Trevi Fountain, the culture/personality clash, the escalating unsanctioned tour (Trastevere rooftop, illegal limoncello, market theft, downpour), and a parting with genuine payoff — the ceramic tile planted in Ben's pocket, which lands the kleptomania motif with wit rather than stating it outright. The show-don't-show handling of Alessandra's stealing (the tile vanishing, the lemon, the tile reappearing warm in Ben's pocket) is the piece's cleverest move, and the ending's ambiguity — is she toying with him, framing him, or gifting him? — honors the prompt's request for enigmatic feelings. Strengths: dialogue is sharp and character-revealing, especially Alessandra's clipped, aphoristic English ("Life is bitter. Coffee reminds you."). The scene structure with timestamps gives momentum. Ben's incremental loosening ("Can burn") is a small but earned beat. Prose is clean and economical, with occasional strong images ("a hornet with a death wish," "moved through the market stalls like water through stone"). Weaknesses: some beats are familiar — the manic-pixie-dream-girl archetype is played straight, the rainstorm huddle is a romance staple, and "something shifted in his chest" is stock phrasing. Alessandra's "You don't want to?" flirtation is a touch on-the-nose. Ben's transformation from flustered academic to willing accomplice happens fast, though the piece at least gestures at his "quiet rebellion" being latent. The Signora Rossi scene is charming but slightly underdeveloped, and the piece runs a bit shorter and sketchier in its middle scenes than the prompt's 1000-word target would fully flesh out. The emotional register stays light; complexity is present but not deep — Alessandra's interiority remains a performance we never see behind, which is arguably intentional but limits emotional resonance. Overall this is skilled, professional commercial fiction: coherent, engaging, well-paced, with only mild cliché and slight thinness of interiority holding it back from the top tier. Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost ## Chapter One: The Quiet Type The gravity hiccups around 20:00 station time. Always does. Old Minh swears it's the centrifuge governor sticking, and I swear he's right, but nobody's bothered to fix it because nobody here cares enough. The whisky in my pour bottle shimmies left, then settles. I wipe the bar down with a rag that's more memory than cloth. "Another?" I ask Old Minh. He waves a hand — all four fingers, which is good for him — and slides his glass back. I pour. The amber liquid trembles as gravity remembers itself. The evening crowd is thin. Two table-hoppers from the merchant vessel *Calico* are sharing fried kelp sticks with Dru, who runs the ore refinery's night shift and has opinions about everything. A knot of miners in the corner plays cards with a deck that's missing the seven of clubs and the Empress of Spades. Someone's jukebox request — something twangy from the old colonies — crackles through speakers that need replacing. It's a Tuesday. Or what passes for Tuesday out here. Quiet. Manageable. Then she walks in. Tentacled dreads — Cephaline, or maybe half — hanging loose and slightly tangled, like she slept wrong or ran hard. Dark jacket, utility grade. Boots that have seen actual dirt, which is unusual for the Outpost. She crosses the floor without looking at anyone and slides onto a stool with the specific exhaustion of someone who's been running from something and has just, in this moment, decided to stop. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." I pull the bottle from the second shelf. Good stuff. Not the best — I save the best for people I know — but respectable. The pour wobbles as gravity stutters again. I slide it across. She drinks half without breathing. Her dreads shift color — pale blue to grey. Stress response. I've seen it before. "Long haul?" I ask. "You could say that." She stares into the glass like it owes her money. I know the type. Actually, I *am* the type. The difference is I've been here three years and she's been here three minutes. I don't push. Pushing is how you lose customers, and I've only got, what, forty regulars? Can't afford to alienate anyone who tips. Dru ambles over, kelp stick in hand. "Fresh face." "Dru," I say. "Don't." "What? I'm being welcoming." She leans on the bar. "I'm Dru. Ore refinery. You are?" The stranger looks at Dru for a long moment. "Passing through." "Through to where?" "Dru." "I'm just making conversation, Nets." Dru grins, but she backs off. She knows the tone. She takes her kelp sticks and returns to the Calico crew, who welcome her back like a returning hero. I polish a glass. The stranger finishes her drink. "Another?" "Please." I pour. The liquid shivers. She wraps both hands around the glass, steadying it — or steadying herself. "I'm Nets," I say. "I run this place." "Nets," she repeats, like she's tasting it. "Short for Nettle?" "Among other things." The corner of her mouth twitches. Not quite a smile. "I'm Sable." "Sable. You want a tab?" "I want to not be found for about six hours." "Can't help you with the first part. The second part, sure. Nobody here asks questions." "Everyone says that." "And yet here you are, asking me questions about saying that." That gets a real smile. Brief, but real. Her dreads flush a soft teal. The door hisses. Two figures enter — broad, deliberate, wearing matching grey jackets with collars up. Not miners. Not merchants. The kind of people who move through a room like they're cataloguing it. My stomach drops. I know hired eyes when I see them. They scan the bar. One of them whispers to the other. Sable's dreads go grey again. She doesn't turn around, but her spine straightens. She's aware of them. "Nets," she says, very quietly. "That back door you definitely have. Does it work?" "It works. But—" "Six hours. That's all I need." The two figures move toward the card game. They're asking questions. Showing something on a tablet. The miners shake their heads. "I don't know what you're running from," I say. "Does it matter?" It doesn't, actually. Or it shouldn't. Three years ago, someone gave me a similar kindness. Old Minh, as a matter of fact. Didn't ask a single question. Just handed me a towel and pointed at the bar. But these two feel different. Professional. The kind of professional that doesn't just *ask* questions. "Nets." Sable's voice is barely above a breath. "Please." The gravity shudders. Glasses across the bar ripple. The jukebox skips a beat. I look at Sable. I look at the two in grey, now talking to Dru, who is helpfully, disastrously, gesturing toward the bar. "Kitchen," I say. "Through the service hatch, left at the compressor, up the maintenance ladder. Takes you to docking level C." "How do I repay—" "You don't. Go." She's gone in a whisper of movement. I grab her glass, wipe the bar, slide a fresh coaster in front of the empty stool. By the time the grey jackets reach me, there's nothing to see but a bartender and a sticky counter. "We're looking for someone," the taller one says. "Aren't we all."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a strong execution of the prompt. It maintains first-person, present tense throughout without slippage, and the dialogue-to-narration ratio sits comfortably near the requested 60%. The cozy sci-fi atmosphere is established efficiently: the gravity hiccups, the missing playing cards, the fried kelp sticks, the jukebox — small, lived-in details that build the world without exposition dumps. The narrator's voice is consistent and appealing: dry, observational, economical. Lines like "a rag that's more memory than cloth" and "she stares into the glass like it owes her money" are memorable without tipping into purple prose. The backstory (Nets was once a fugitive herself, saved by Old Minh's kindness) is delivered in a single compact paragraph — show-adjacent, well-placed, and it motivates her decision to help Sable without belaboring it. Conflict is established clearly and left unresolved: the grey-jacketed pursuers arrive, Sable escapes through the kitchen, and the chapter ends mid-confrontation with "Aren't we all." This satisfies the instruction not to resolve the conflict, and the cliffhanger generates genuine forward momentum. Character actions are believable. Sable's paranoia, color-shifting dreads as stress tells, and clipped speech all cohere. Dru's nosiness is a natural, slightly predictable complication — her gesturing toward the bar is a well-chosen small betrayal that raises stakes. The pursuers are archetypal (mysterious figures in matching grey jackets) but functional for a chapter one. Weaknesses: the pursuers are stock figures, and the "professional hunters arrive at the exact bar" timing is convenient. Sable's name and situation are deliberately withheld, which is fine, but her characterization leans on type (the tired fugitive) more than distinct individuality. The banter ("And yet here you are, asking me questions about saying that") is good but flirts with being a touch too clever. The prose occasionally leans on familiar beats — "spine straightens," "stomach drops" — but these are minor. Nothing is overwrought, meandering, or amateurish; the piece is disciplined, well-paced, and tonally unified. Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom).
