+ First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection She texted back in nine minutes last time. Today it took her an hour and forty. An hour and forty to write *sounds good, see you at 7 :)* A smiley face. Not even an emoji. A colon and a parenthesis, which is either nothing or everything, and I'm supposed to know which. Okay. Okay. So she's pulling back. That's what this is. I can feel it starting, the way you feel weather change in your scars. Two weeks ago she fell asleep with her hand on my chest and said *I love being here* and I replayed it so many times the words started to lose meaning, like saying your own name until it sounds foreign. I should have known. That was the peak. That was the top of the hill, and everything since has been the slow roll down. She'll sit across from me tonight. She'll be warm but different-warm. Polite-warm. She'll say *we should talk* and I'll say *about what* even though I'll know exactly about what, and she'll say *I really care about you* — note the present tense, note the *care* instead of *love*, note how she'll touch her napkin instead of my hand — *but I need to be honest about where I'm at right now.* And I'll say: *Where you're at.* And she'll say: *I just think we moved really fast and I—* *Moved fast. Okay. So now it's fast. Now that you've gotten what you—* No. No, don't do that. That's the thing. That's the thing you do. You go cold before they even get the chance. But she will get the chance. That's the problem. She'll get the chance and I'll be standing there with all my rehearsals useless because the real thing never matches the script. The real thing is always worse because in the real thing you can't pause and think of the perfect devastating line. In the real thing your face does things you can't control. Let me try again. She'll say *I care about you* and I'll say *then why did it take you an hour and forty minutes to answer a text about dinner.* And she'll look confused, and I'll feel the confusion is fake, and I'll say *you used to answer in minutes, Elise, so something changed, and I'd rather you just tell me than make me guess.* She'll say *I was in a meeting.* A meeting. Sure. She'll say *I told you about the quarterly review, remember? Tuesday and Thursday afternoons?* And she'll be right. She did say that. Last week she mentioned it, and I said *that sounds brutal* and she laughed and said *you have no idea* and I felt useful, felt needed, felt like I was something she carried into her difficult day. But maybe she mentioned the meeting so she'd have an alibi. Maybe she planted it. People do that. People build their exits early. No — I know that's not real. I know that. I can see myself building the case and I can see that the case is made of nothing. She mentioned a meeting. She had a meeting. These are just facts. But facts don't help. Facts are small and quiet and the fear is huge and loud and the fear says *she touched her phone and saw your name and thought not yet, not yet, I'll deal with her later.* Her. Deal with *her.* That's how she thinks of me. Something to deal with. I'm doing it again. I can see myself doing it. It's like watching your hands shake and not being able to stop them. I know the pattern. I've named the pattern. I've said the word *borderline* out loud in a therapist's office and felt the relief of taxonomy. But naming a hurricane doesn't make it stop spinning. She called me yesterday. Not texted. Called. And when I picked up she said *I just wanted to hear your voice,* and my whole chest opened up, I mean physically opened, like a door I didn't know was locked, and I thought: she loves me. She actually loves me. And then immediately, so fast it was almost the same thought: *why.* Why does she want to hear my voice. What does she need. What is she setting up. Nobody just calls. Nobody just wants to hear your voice. That's something people say in movies before they leave. I said *hey* and she said *hey, how's your day* and I said *it's fine* and she said *just fine?* and there was so much warmth in her voice, so much genuine curiosity, and I wanted to crawl through the phone and live in that warmth. I wanted to say *my day is horrible because I've spent it imagining twelve different versions of you leaving me and every single one felt real.* I wanted to say *please don't go, I know that's crazy, I know you haven't said you're going, but please don't go.* I said *yeah, just a long day.* She said *I'm sorry. Can I do anything?* And I thought: yes, you can never change. You can stay exactly this warm forever. You can never have a bad day, never be tired, never be distracted, never take an hour and forty minutes to answer a text, because I will read every deviation as the beginning of the end and I will not survive it. I said *you're already doing it.* She said *good. I like doing it.* And I hung up and cried because it was so beautiful and so impossible. Because no one can carry that. No one can be the thing I need them to be, which is: constant. Unshakeable. Mine in a way that proves I exist. I'm walking to the restaurant now. I left early because I couldn't stay in my apartment with my thoughts. But my thoughts came with me. They always come with me. I pass the hallway mirror and catch a glimpse — shoulders up near my ears, jaw set, eyes already arguing with someone who hasn't spoken yet. I look like I'm bracing for impact. I look like a person who has already been hit. I turn away from the mirror. She'll be at the table. She'll smile. It will be real and I will not believe it. Or I'll believe it for three seconds and then I'll wonder why it's that particular smile, that angle, and what it means that she smiled *before* I sat down instead of after, and whether that means she's relieved I'm here or relieved this is almost over. I'll sit down. I'll say *hey.* She'll say *hey* back and reach for my hand. And I'll let her take it. And I'll spend the entire dinner trying to feel her grip loosening. --- She's already here. She's waving. She's standing up. She's hugging me before I even reach the table. *Hi,* she says. *I missed you today.* And for one second — one perfect, terrible second — I believe her.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece executes the prompt's difficult brief with notable skill. The internal monologue form is sustained almost entirely, as requested, and the cycling between anticipated rejection, rehearsed confrontation, and preemptive resentment is rendered convincingly. The imagined dialogues with Elise are sharply differentiated from real interactions, and the narrator's selective self-awareness ("I can see myself building the case and I can see that the case is made of nothing") captures the requested cognitive dissonance without resolving it too neatly. Strengths: the text-message timing opening is an excellent concrete trigger; the "quarterly review" detail grounds the paranoia in verifiable fact the narrator dismisses; the phone call scene delivers genuine warmth that is immediately questioned, exactly as specified. The prose is controlled and rhythmic, with strong images ("I look like a person who has already been hit," "naming a hurricane doesn't make it stop spinning"). The ending lands the dissonance rather than a false cure. Weaknesses: a few lines edge toward the aphoristic and slightly over-polished ("the relief of taxonomy," "a door I didn't know was locked"), which risks feeling writerly rather than thought. The "constant, unshakeable, mine in a way that proves I exist" passage states the pathology a touch too explicitly — a mild tell-don't-show lapse in an otherwise shown piece. The real Elise is thin (functional rather than dimensional), though this is arguably appropriate to a monologue. The word count is somewhat under 1000. The pattern-recognition moments occasionally arrive a beat too articulately, making the narrator slightly more insightful than the "limited and selective" awareness requested, though the piece does show the insight failing to interrupt the pattern. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 71.7
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The abandoned temple of Tuolizhen had not heard prayer in forty years. Tonight, it heard money—coins slapping palms, voices cutting through incense-thick air, bodies pressing against crumbling pillars to watch two men settle what their grandfathers should have buried. Tatsuya Mori stood near the temple's northern wall, beneath a roof beam where centuries of rain had carved dark veins into the wood. His red-and-black armband bore the crossed-sword crest of Jigen-ryū, tied tight above his left elbow. He held a bokken—white oak, straight, unadorned—angled across his chest in the signature Jigen chamber. His weight sat coiled on his rear foot, front knee slightly bent, shoulders squared toward his opponent like a loaded cannon. Twelve meters south, beneath the temple's empty altar platform, Chen Wenzhou rolled his neck in slow, unhurried circles. His armband carried the embroidered palm-fan insignia of his Piguaquan lineage. He held nothing. His arms hung loose at his sides, fingers slightly curled, wrists soft as silk ropes. His stance was narrow—weight distributed evenly, knees barely bent, body angled sideways to present a thinner profile. Between them, the temple floor was cracked stone, swept clean of debris by someone who cared enough about the fight to remove the tripping hazards. The crowd numbered perhaps thirty. Jigen students occupied the eastern pillars, their silence disciplined, almost liturgical. Chen's people clustered along the western wall—louder, shifting, passing a clay jug between them. The wagering had already concluded. Everything that could be staked had been staked. A woman near the altar—a neutral party, known only as the Bell—raised her hand. Both fighters' eyes locked. Her hand fell. Tatsuya closed the distance in three explosive steps. His bokken rose from its chambered position in a single vertical strike—a Jigen *kirioroshi*—descending with the full rotational force of his hips and a sharp exhalation that echoed off the temple walls. The strike aimed to split Chen from crown to sternum. It was not a testing blow. It was a killing stroke delivered at full commitment, because Jigen-ryū recognized no other kind. Chen pivoted on his left foot, body rotating clockwise. The bokken hissed past his right shoulder, close enough to disturb the fabric of his shirt. His right arm—relaxed until the precise moment of contact—whipped upward in a Pigua palm strike, the heel of his hand catching Tatsuya's right wrist. The deflection was minimal, economical, redirecting rather than blocking. The bokken's momentum carried Tatsuya's strike past its target and slightly forward, his weight tipping onto his front foot. Chen's left palm immediately followed, arcing in a horizontal sweep toward Tatsuya's exposed ribs. Tatsuya recovered with startling speed, yanking the bokken back in a sharp reverse cut that forced Chen to retreat two quick steps. The wooden blade grazed Chen's forearm—not enough to damage, enough to sting. They reset. Eight meters between them now. Tatsuya attacked again. This time, a lateral strike—a horizontal slash aimed at Chen's midsection, generated from a violent hip rotation that made his hakama snap like a flag in wind. Chen dropped low, bending at the knees rather than the waist, and the bokken passed over his head with centimeters to spare. From his crouched position, Chen's right arm whipped outward in a Pigua *pi* strike—an outward chopping palm that targeted Tatsuya's leading knee. Tatsuya withdrew his front leg and brought the bokken down in a thrust, aiming for Chen's exposed back. Chen rolled laterally across the stone floor, coming up on both feet three meters to Tatsuya's left, now positioned at an angle rather than directly in front. The Jigen students made no sound. Chen's people roared. Tatsuya turned to face the new angle, recalibrated, and pressed forward. He launched a rapid sequence—three strikes in under two seconds. A diagonal downward cut, a reverse upward slash, and a straight thrust. Each was delivered with total commitment, each designed to end the fight. There was no combination strategy in Jigen-ryū—only a series of decisive blows, each treated as the final one. Chen intercepted the diagonal cut with a *gua*—an inward sweeping block using the outer edge of his forearm, redirecting the bokken across his body. The reverse slash he avoided by shifting his weight backward, his feet sliding on the stone. The thrust he caught with both palms, clapping together on the bokken's shaft just below the tsuba. For one breath, they were locked—Tatsuya pushing forward, Chen holding the blade stationary. Tatsuya's arms trembled with effort. Chen's face showed nothing except concentration, his feet sliding back centimeter by centimeter as the force drove him toward the western wall. Then Chen's right foot hooked behind Tatsuya's leading ankle—a trip executed not with strength but with timing and positioning. Tatsuya stumbled, his grip on the bokken loosening for a fraction of a second. Chen wrenched the weapon sideways, not to disarm but to create an opening, and drove his left palm upward into Tatsuya's solar plexus. The impact was not a push. It was a detonation—Pigua power generated through the sequential whipping of shoulder, elbow, and wrist. Tatsuya's feet left the ground. He landed on his back two meters behind where he'd been standing, the bokken clattering from his grip, spinning across the stone. Silence. Tatsuya rose. Blood traced his lower lip. He retrieved the bokken without breaking eye contact. His breathing was ragged but his stance reformed instantly—weapon chambered, weight coiled, shoulders square. Chen raised both palms, fingers spread, the traditional Pigua guard. His own breathing was elevated now. The palm strike had cost him energy. His left shoulder—where the first grazing cut had landed—was beginning to stiffen. They circled. Slowly. The crowd had stopped breathing. Tatsuya feinted high and drove a low thrust at Chen's abdomen. Chen parried with a downward *gua* and countered with a right palm strike to the jaw. Tatsuya ducked beneath it and delivered a rising cut that caught Chen across the chest—not the blade, but the flat, delivered with enough force to crack ribs. Chen staggered backward, arm folded across his chest. He did not retreat further. Instead, he advanced. What followed was Piguaquan in its purest expression—both arms whipping in continuous alternating arcs, palms striking from angles that seemed to violate geometry. Overhead, lateral, upward, inward. Each strike flowed into the next without pause, creating a rotating sphere of violence around Chen's body that Tatsuya could not enter without being struck. Tatsuya parried desperately, the bokken moving faster than it had all night, deflecting strikes that came from his blind spots. A palm clipped his temple. Another caught his sword hand. A third—the decisive one—struck the inside of his right elbow, hyperextending the joint. The bokken fell. Chen's final palm stopped one centimeter from Tatsuya's throat. The temple held its silence for three heartbeats. Then both sides erupted—shouting, cursing, coins changing hands. Tatsuya stared at the palm hovering before his neck. His jaw worked. Pride and fury warred behind his eyes. He stepped back. Bowed—shallow, rigid, barely compliant. Chen lowered his arm, cradling his injured ribs, and returned the bow with equal stiffness. The blood debt between their schools would not be settled tonight. But it had been added to.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, tightly choreographed fight scene that fulfills the prompt's core requirements well. The physical coherence demanded by the instructions is largely maintained: the piece tracks distances ("twelve meters south," "eight meters between them"), positions relative to walls and pillars, and the mechanics of each exchange with unusual precision. The opening establishes the arena spatially—northern wall, altar platform, eastern and western factions—which gives subsequent movement a legible map. The stylistic contrast between the two arts is effectively rendered through action rather than exposition for the most part: Jigen-ryū as single decisive killing strokes, Piguaquan as whipping redirection and circular counters. The set-piece moments work—the mutual lock on the bokken, the ankle hook, the "rotating sphere of violence" finale—are vivid and mechanically plausible. Weaknesses: the characters are thin. Tatsuya and Chen are styles first, people second; their "hot-headed" nature and "simmering animosity" is asserted by the premise rather than dramatized—no dialogue, no interiority, no personal history beyond the school rivalry. The crowd is atmospheric but generic. The prose occasionally leans on formulaic constructions ("It was not a push. It was a detonation—"), and some sentences have a clipped, list-like rhythm that reads as efficient rather than elegant. The ending is appropriately restrained—no false reconciliation—but the final line ("it had been added to") is a neat, slightly pat button. The piece is disciplined and coherent but emotionally shallow; it engages as spectacle, not as story. There is no dialogue, so that criterion is excluded. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The speakers in all four corners hit the downbeat like a fist to the sternum. Same chorus, same BPM, same surgically enhanced pop track I'd heard 200 times this week—but from four directions at once, the sound folding over itself until the studio became a pressure chamber. "From the top," Instructor Kang said. She stood at the front wall between the mirror and the window, arms crossed, one hand still holding the clicker she used to mark mistakes. Each click carved a notch into the air. "Positions." Thirty-one bodies snapped to formation. I snapped too—late by half a count, because my body wanted to find the groove first, wanted to roll through the balls of my feet and let the music settle into my chest before I committed. That's how we danced at home: listen, feel, then move. Here, you moved when the clock told you to. We were in a diamond formation, four rows deep. I stood third row, stage left, between Min-jun—a sixteen-year-old from Busan who'd been training since he could walk—and Sora, whose extension was so clean it looked computer-generated. I could see myself in the mirror, sandwiched between their identical postures. My shoulders were wrong. Too loose. My weight sat differently, hovering over my center like I was ready to break in any direction, because that's what the concrete had taught me: stay mobile, stay ready, stay alive. The choreography was a K-pop title track called "Vanguard." Military concept. The opening sequence required eight counts of synchronized marching—stomp right, stomp left, pivot quarter-turn outward, arms locked at ninety degrees, wrists snapped flat. Then a ripple pass from center outward, each row peeling away in a wave. Kang clicked her tongue. "Row three. Your arms are descending at different rates. Sora, you're early. Marcus—" She said my name the way she said everything: like she was identifying a specimen. "—your left arm is sweeping. It should be cutting." I knew what she meant. In hip-hop, a sweep carries weight. You move through the space, letting the arm pull the torso, letting the torso shift the hips. It's a chain reaction. But here, the arm moved independently—locked at the shoulder, elbow, wrist. A machine part. No chain. No reaction. "Again," she said. The music restarted. I counted internally—one, two, three, four—and drove my arm forward, trying to make it a blade instead of a wave. My tricep burned from the unfamiliar isolation. At count five, the pivot turn, my feet betrayed me. Instead of the clean quarter-turn on the ball of my right foot, my body slipped into a salsa step—a cross-body lead, weight transferring left-right-left—that I'd learned from my mother in our kitchen when I was seven. The muscle memory was so deep it lived below thought. Min-jun's elbow nearly clipped mine. The ripple pass collapsed. Three people behind me stumbled out of sync. Kang didn't click. She just watched in the mirror. "Marcus. Stay after." The others exhaled. I felt their relief like a weather pattern—thirty bodies decompressing, dropping their shoulders, shuffling to the back wall for water bottles. Min-jun touched my elbow as he passed. A small mercy. When the studio emptied, Kang walked to the center of the floor. She was maybe fifty, maybe older—her face had the ageless quality of someone who'd spent decades controlling it. She'd been a principal dancer in a company I'd never heard of, then a choreographer for groups I'd grown up watching on a cracked phone screen. "Show me something," she said. "What?" "Whatever you were doing before you came here. The real thing. Thirty seconds." The speakers were off. The silence was enormous. I stood at center. My body knew what to do without music—it had learned in silence before, on the basketball court behind the bodega, on the platform where the 4 train never came on time. I breathed in, dropped my weight into my hips, and let go. A sweep—arms carving wide arcs, chest rolling through the motion. My feet found a six-step break, legs threading through each other, weight shifting from hands to feet to shoulders as I dropped into a freeze, held it, then flowed upward into a wave that traveled from my fingertips through my collarbone and rippled down my spine. I added a thread—the leg weaving through the arms—and came up into a body roll that ended with my chin tilted toward the fluorescent lights. It was ugly and beautiful and mine. Kang watched without expression. Then she walked to the front wall and stood beside the mirror, arms crossed. "You have something that cannot be taught," she said. "And something that must be unlearned." "Which is which?" "Your body speaks. That's the gift. But it speaks whatever it wants, whenever it wants. In formation, that's noise. Thirty bodies speaking at once, each in its own language—that's not a performance. That's chaos." "So I just—what—shut up?" Kang uncrossed her arms. She walked to the second speaker, the one stage left, and turned it off. Then the one behind me. Then the other two. The studio went quiet. "You learn grammar," she said. "Then you learn to break it deliberately. But first, grammar." She restarted only the front-left speaker. The track played at half volume, tinny and small. "Run the march. Alone. I'll watch from the back." I took my position at center. The beat dropped, and I marched—stomp, stomp, pivot, arms locked. My left arm swept. I caught it, corrected, overcorrected. My feet wanted the salsa step. I denied them. Eight counts. Sixteen. Thirty-two. At the ripple pass, alone, there was no one to ripple to. Just me, cutting the air with arms that didn't know how to cut. Kang watched from the back wall, silhouette against the afternoon light. "Again," she said. And I knew—standing there, sweat already soaking through the academy-issued shirt that fit wrong across my shoulders—that this was the real audition. Not the scholarship tape. Not the first week. This. The moment where I either learned to speak their language or went home still fluent in mine. I reset. The beat dropped. I marched.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong competence. Physical coherence is well maintained: the diamond formation, row positions, the failed pivot into a salsa cross-body lead, the ripple collapse, and the solo re-run are all spatially trackable. The contrast between street and commercial styles is rendered through concrete technical detail (sweep vs. cut, isolations vs. chain reactions, six-step, thread, freeze, wave). The muscle-memory betrayal moment (salsa step surfacing mid-pivot) is the strongest beat—specific, believable, and thematically loaded. Kang is a familiar archetype (the severe instructor who sees raw talent), and her "grammar" speech is well-written but predictable; the piece doesn't subvert the trope. The dialogue is functional and mostly sharp ("Which is which?" is a good exchange), though Kang's lines edge toward aphorism. The ending—choosing to march—is an honest decision point, but it resolves slightly toward compliance without fully dramatizing the cost; still, the closing "I marched" carries appropriate ambivalence rather than false triumph. Prose is clean and controlled, with a few excellent images ("Each click carved a notch into the air," "relief like a weather pattern"). Occasionally it leans on neat formulations ("It was ugly and beautiful and mine") that flirt with the overwrought without crossing over. Internal monologue delivers culture shock and class anxiety effectively through concrete detail (cracked phone screen, the 4 train, the bodega court) rather than exposition. Weaknesses: the narrative arc is conventional—talented outsider humbled by stern mentor is well-trodden; the "stay after class" pivot is expected the moment it's announced. The stakes of losing one's authentic voice are stated more than deeply explored; the piece gestures at it but the solo freestyle resolves the tension too comfortably. Minor physical nit: "third row, stage left" of a diamond is slightly ambiguous but forgivable. Overall: a disciplined, vivid, professional piece that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision, held back from excellence by its predictability of arc and a somewhat safe resolution. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute The sand in the great hourglass fell upward, sometimes. Dream had never bothered to fix this. He found it kept petitioners anxious, which was the general idea. He sat in the high chair, his face the sort of beautiful that made people forget what they'd been saying. Today this was a mercy, because what they'd been saying was tedious in the extreme. "Approach," he said, and the word settled over the chamber like a held breath. First Love approached. He was pink. Everything about him was pink—his cheeks, his curling hair, the faint luminescence that clung to him like dawn on a windowsill. He clutched a sheaf of dream-templates to his chest as though they might be stolen, which, in the Dreaming, they frequently were. "Your Endlessness," he began, his voice cracking with the particular earnestness of someone who had never once been sued, "I have cultivated this dreamspace for eleven months. Eleven. Do you know how long it takes to calibrate the exact shade of wildflower? The precise *angle* of sunlight that suggests hope without becoming saccharine?" "Get to the point," said Dream. "The defendant—" First Love pointed a trembling finger "—*squatting*." Mora sat in the defendant's crag. She was dark where First Love was bright, angular where he was soft. She wore the shape of a woman the way one wears a borrowed coat—close enough, but the sleeves didn't quite match. Her eyes were the yellow of old teeth. She had crossed her legs and was examining her nails with the studied disinterest of someone who knows she's already won. "I prefer *adverse possession*," she said. "Squatting is so common." "You *are* common," First Love sputtered. "You're a—she's a chest-sitter, Your Endlessness! A suffocator! She doesn't even have zoning clearance for romantic dreamscapes! Her jurisdiction is strictly night-terrors, sleep paralysis, and—" he consulted his notes "—'ambiguous nocturnal dread, category three or higher.'" "I have range," said Mora. Dream closed his eyes. He could feel a headache building, which was impressive for an anthropomorphic concept. He glanced at the hourglass. The sand had stopped entirely, which meant the court stenographer (a moth with spectacles) had fallen asleep. "The specifics," Dream said. "Now." First Love produced a dream-fragment in a jar, shaking it until it illuminated. Inside, a boy lay in a field of flowers beside a girl with dark hair. The sky was golden. The girl leaned close. The boy's face held that particular agony of wanting something you don't yet have words for. "Beautiful," First Love whispered. "Perfect. The almost-kiss—the *confusion*—that's my signature. That's my *craft*." "And then," Dream prompted. First Love shook the jar again. The scene shifted. The girl mounted the boy playfully, as she always did in this iteration—but then her face *changed*. Her jaw extended. Her eyes went yellow. She settled her weight on his chest and leaned down, and the boy's expression shifted from pleasant confusion to genuine terror, though—and First Love stamped his foot here—*not entirely* terror, which was somehow worse. "You see what she's done?" First Love cried. "She's corrupted the emotional palette! He's frightened but he's also still—it's a *muddle*! That muddle is *my* intellectual property!" Mora stood. The temperature dropped. "A girl's gotta eat," she said simply. "You know how it is. Or perhaps you don't, being a concept and all. But the boy—Max, lovely boy, terrible sleep hygiene—he's got energy. Real *juice*. The fear is good, I won't deny it, but the desire underneath?" She made a sound that wasn't quite a moan and wasn't quite a purr. "That's the meal. That's the whole meal. Fear alone is bread. Fear mixed with wanting? That's *cake*." "You admit to the incursion?" Dream asked. "I admit to nothing. I admit to *dining*." She smiled. Her teeth were too many. "Besides, he dreamed the door open. She climbs on top of him every cycle—that's *your* design, Rosy. I just walked through the door he built." First Love made a sound like a kettle dying. Dream considered. He could rule for First Love. Restore the dream. Simple, clean, forgettable. The boy would have his flowers and his almost-kiss and grow up to write mediocre poetry about it. He could rule for Mora. Let the nightmare feast. The boy would wake gasping, confused, eventually develop a complex about dark-haired women that would take years of therapy to unpack. Not Dream's concern. But. Dream's mouth twitched. It was not a smile. Dream did not smile. It was merely a facial arrangement that suggested, to those who knew him, that someone was about to suffer in an interesting way. "A compromise," he said. Both parties stiffened. "The dreamscape remains shared," Dream continued. "First Love retains narrative architecture. Mora retains feeding rights. However—" and here he paused, because drama was the one indulgence he permitted himself "—the transformation occurs at the *exact moment of the almost-kiss.* Not before. Not after. The girl changes as their lips nearly meet. The terror and the desire become... simultaneous. Permanent. Inseparable." First Love went pale. "That's—" "Artistic collaboration," said Dream. "I'm told it's very enriching." Mora's yellow eyes narrowed. Then, slowly, she began to laugh. It was the sound of something breaking in a dark room. "I accept," she said. "I don't—" First Love started. "You do," said Dream. "Or I revoke your crafting license and reassign you to anxiety dreams about missing buses." The sand resumed falling. The moth woke up. "Next case," said Dream. He was not smiling. He was never smiling. But somewhere, a boy named Max was about to have a very interesting night.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the brief with considerable skill. Dream's irritation is established economically ("Today this was a mercy, because what they'd been saying was tedious in the extreme"), and the courtroom-fantasy collision generates consistent comedy: the moth stenographer falling asleep, zoning clearance for romantic dreamscapes, "adverse possession" vs. "squatting." The upward-falling hourglass is a nice worldbuilding touch that doubles as characterization. Mora is the standout: her "fear is bread, fear mixed with wanting is cake" speech is genuinely funny and sinister, and her legalistic deflection ("I admit to dining") lands well. First Love's pink earnestness and the kettle-dying sound are effective farce. Dream's temptation toward mischief is realized in the compromise ruling, which is both cruel and thematically apt—fusing terror and desire permanently is exactly the kind of interesting suffering the prompt requested. Weaknesses: some jokes are over-explained. "It was not a smile. Dream did not smile" is repeated nearly verbatim at the end, and the narrator underlines the joke both times rather than trusting the reader. "Someone was about to suffer in an interesting way" is good, but the closing "He was not smiling. He was never smiling" hammers it. The "not entirely terror, which was somehow worse" beat is strong but slightly over-narrated. The prose occasionally reaches for cleverness that borders on cute ("the particular earnestness of someone who had never once been sued" is good; "the sort of beautiful that made people forget what they'd been saying" is fine but a touch self-satisfied). The ending's "very interesting night" is a mild anticlimax after the strong ruling. Structure is tight, no meandering, dialogue is crisp and differentiated. Tone is consistently dry and dark. Word count near target. Descriptives used sparingly as instructed. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, hinting at a hurried departure. The village itself is empty—not the emptiness of the recently dead, but the deeper emptiness of a place that has been *chosen* by something that feeds. Yennefer smells the blood before she sees him. It hangs in the air like perfume gone wrong—copper and rot and something older beneath, something that predates the villages and the cart wheels and the desperate fleeing. She stops in the center of the muddy street, her heels sinking slightly, and lets the darkness collect around her shoulders like a shawl. "You're not what I came here to kill," she says to the empty air. The laughter comes from everywhere. "That depends, sorceress." The voice is rich, dark, amused. It rolls across the rooftops and through the broken windows of the cottages. "On what you came here to kill. And on what kills you first." He materializes from shadow itself—one moment the street is empty, the next he is *there*, tall and angular, his red coat flaring in a wind that doesn't exist. The wide-brimmed hat casts his face in darkness. The orange lenses of his glasses catch the blood moon overhead and throw it back doubled. Yennefer does not step back. She does not flinch. She has faced djinns and wild hunt riders and the inside of her own worst memories. She will not flinch for a vampire in a ridiculous coat. "You've been busy," she observes, gesturing to the dark stains that streak the cobblestones. "Thirty, forty villagers? And you left them strung up like livestock. Tacky." "Tacky." He tilts his head. The grin that spreads across his face has too many teeth. "I haven't heard that word in three hundred years. I think I've missed it." He moves. Not walks—*moves*, a liquid displacement of space that puts him ten feet closer without any visible transition. Yennefer's fingers spark violet at her sides. Chaos gathers in her palms like held breath. "Stop." He stops. He seems genuinely delighted. "You can command me?" "I can command anything stupid enough to listen." The grin widens. "Oh, I *like* you." He removes his hat, sweeps a bow that belongs in a court that no longer exists. "Alucard. At your service. Or rather—" he straightens, and for a moment the shadows behind him writhe with eyes, "—at theirs." The eyes blink. Dozens. Hundreds. They watch her from the walls, from the ground, from the inside of her own peripheral vision. Yennefer's stomach turns. She keeps her face still through centuries of practice. "A vampire who plays with his food," she says. "How original." "A sorceress who hides her deformity with magic," he replies, and the words land like a slap. Her violet eyes flash. The air between them *cracks* with raw Chaos, and a bolt of compressed force tears through the space where his chest should be. It punches through him, exits through his back, shatters the door of the cottage behind him into splinters. Alucard looks down at the hole in his torso. The darkness inside it writhes. "Magnificent," he breathes. The wound seals. Not heals—*seals*, flesh crawling back together like water filling a vessel. He rolls his shoulders and the coat is whole again, as if reality itself has been bullied into compliance. Yennefer stares. She has seen regeneration. She has never seen *this*. "What are you?" "Old," he says. "Older than your magic. Older than the words you'd use to bind me." He steps closer. She holds her ground. The smell of lilac and gooseberries meets the smell of blood. "Older than the thing inside you that you pretend doesn't ache." "Don't." "I can smell it, you know. The absence. The hollow where something should grow." His voice drops to something almost gentle. "Does it keep you awake? That empty room in your body?" Her hand comes up. Chaos spirals around her fingers, black and violet, a spell that could unmake the village and everything in it. Her arm trembles—not with fear, but with the effort of holding back. "You know nothing about me." "I know you're in pain. I know you'd burn the world to fill that space. I know you're too proud to ask for help even from someone who could give it." He removes his glasses. His eyes are red and fathomless. "I know because I am the same." The spell dissipates. They stand in the blood moon light, the sorceress and the vampire, and for one long moment neither of them moves. The village holds its breath around them. Then Yennefer laughs—short, bitter, genuine. "You're a poet." "I'm a monster." "Those aren't mutually exclusive." He puts his glasses back on. His hat follows. The shadows settle. "The villagers," she says. "Did you kill them all?" "Most. Some fled. Some hid." He gestures vaguely toward the church at the end of the street. "One is still alive in there. Praying. I've been saving her." "For what?" "For someone worth sharing a meal with." Yennefer looks at the church. Looks at him. Makes a decision she'll question for centuries. "I don't share meals with vampires." "Then come and watch me eat. And tell me about the hollow. And I'll tell you about mine." He extends a gloved hand. She doesn't take it. But she walks beside him.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding crossover prompt. The prose is controlled, atmospheric, and consistently present-tense third person as instructed. The opening establishes dread efficiently—the empty village, the blood smell—and the pacing of the Alucard reveal is well handled, with his shadow-materialization and the eyes in the darkness capturing his Hellsing menace without over-explaining. Character work is the piece's greatest strength. Alucard's theatricality, regeneration, and hunger for a worthy opponent are all present and accurate; his delight at being commanded ("You can command me?") is a genuinely in-character beat. Yennefer's refusal to flinch, her sarcasm ("Tacky"), and above all the wound Alucard strikes at her infertility are faithful to her source. The moment where he names "the hollow" is the emotional core of the story—cruel, perceptive, and it earns the shift in their dynamic. Her spell dissipating rather than striking a second time is a believable, restrained choice. Weaknesses: the ending is the riskiest part. Yennefer walking beside him toward a church where he's "saving" a villager to share a meal is dark and in-character for Alucard, but Yennefer's acquiescence—"tell me about the hollow. And I'll tell you about mine"—moves slightly fast, a mild unearned intimacy after one conversation. It's not a full transformation, and her refusal to take his hand preserves her pride, but the final beat edges toward romanticized darkness. The "I am the same" line is a touch on-the-nose, and Alucard's knowledge of her infertility is convenient (though vampires reading bodies is plausible enough). Some phrases ("reality itself has been bullied into compliance") flirt with cleverness but mostly land. The piece is somewhat predictable in structure—power display, verbal sparring, mutual recognition—but the execution elevates the familiar shape. Dialogue is sharp throughout, with distinct voices. Prose is polished without tipping into purple. Emotionally, the piece achieves genuine complexity: revulsion, fascination, pain, and a bitter kinship. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 55.5
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Jolyne Cujoh has learned to read those rattles like a language—who's walking heavy with intent, who's shuffling defeated, who's about to start something. Three weeks in this place, and her survival instincts have sharpened. But the woman walking toward her makes no sound at all. Jolyne looks up from the bench where she's been pretending to read, her fingers already twitching with the instinct to summon Stone Free. The newcomer wears a crisp suit that has no business in a prison yard, auburn hair falling perfectly despite the afternoon wind. Her eyes are wrong—ringed like tree rings, yellow. "Jolyne Cujoh." The woman's voice is soft, pleasant, like she's offering tea instead of standing in a yard full of murderers. "I'm Makima. I've been assigned as a special counselor to this facility." "Never heard of counselors who dress like government spooks." Jolyne doesn't stand. Doesn't offer her hand. Her butterfly tattoo itches beneath her sleeve. "What do you want?" "Just to talk." Makima smiles, and it's perfect. Too perfect. Every muscle in Jolyne's back tightens. "I've read your file. Framed for a crime you didn't commit. Abandoned by your father. You must feel so alone." The words land like slaps, but Jolyne doesn't flinch. "You read a file. Congratulations. You want a medal?" Makima tilts her head, that smile never wavering. "I want to help you. I have a certain... talent for helping people who've been discarded." Something in her tone makes Jolyne's skin crawl. She's met manipulators before—in this prison, on the streets, in her own family. But Makima operates on a frequency she can't quite identify, like a radio station broadcasting just outside human range. "Yeah? What's the catch?" "No catch. Just cooperation." Makima takes a step closer, and the inmates nearest them instinctively move away, like fish parting around a shark. "I understand you have an unusual ability. Something beyond normal human capability." Jolyne's jaw tightens. "I don't know what you're talking about." "Of course you do." Makima's ringed eyes hold Jolyne's gaze, and there's a weight behind them—ancient, hungry. "I can sense it. You carry something inside you. Something that could be very valuable." The fence rattles. Someone's coming, but Jolyne doesn't look away from Makima. She can't. Those eyes are pulling at something in her chest, something that wants to agree, to submit, to kneel. *Fuck that.* "You know," Jolyne says, standing slowly, "my dad's an asshole who couldn't be bothered to visit me once. My mom checked out years ago. Every friend I've ever had has either betrayed me or died." She lets Stone Free shimmer at the edge of manifestation, strings curling around her fingertips like warning signs. "So when someone like you walks up talking about helping me, I know you're full of shit." Makima's smile doesn't crack, but something shifts behind her eyes. Interest. Calculation. "You're perceptive," she says. "More so than the others." "The others?" "The other inmates. The guards. The warden." Makima gestures vaguely at the yard. "They've all been so cooperative. So eager to please. But you..." She studies Jolyne like a specimen. "You're different. There's something in you that refuses to be controlled." Jolyne laughs, sharp and humorless. "Lady, you have no idea." "I'd like to." Makima steps closer again, and now Jolyne can feel it—a pressure against her mind, like fingers trying to pry open a locked door. "I could give you everything you want. Freedom from this place. Your father's attention. Revenge against everyone who wronged you. All you have to do is accept me." The offer hits harder than Jolyne expects. For one terrible second, she can see it—walking out of these gates, making Jotaro look at her with something other than disappointment, watching her enemies bleed. The vision is so sweet it aches. Then she thinks about her mother's face. About the look in Jotaro's eyes when he does show up—guilty, distant, but *there*. About Hermes and Foo Fighters, the only people in this shithole who've earned her trust. "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney," Jolyne mutters. Makima blinks. "Excuse me?" "You're selling me a fantasy." Jolyne lets Stone Free manifest fully now, strings spreading across the yard like a web, connecting to fences, benches, walls. "I've been manipulated by experts. My ex-boyfriend framed me for murder. My father abandoned me for years. But at least they were honest about being selfish." She wraps a string around Makima's wrist, thin as spider silk and strong as steel. "You're something worse. You actually believe you're offering me a gift." Makima looks down at the string. Her expression remains pleasant, but her eyes have changed—colder, older, evaluating. "Interesting," she says. "You can resist." "I can do a lot of things." Jolyne pulls the string taut. "Now here's what's going to happen. You're going to stay away from me and anyone I care about in this prison. You're going to take your government spook suit and your dead eyes and your creepy smile, and you're going to find someone else to play your games with." "And if I don't?" Jolyne grins, all teeth. "Then we find out what happens when an unstoppable force meets an unbreakable string." For a long moment, Makima doesn't move. The yard has gone silent. Even the fences have stopped rattling. Then Makima laughs—soft, genuine, and somehow more unsettling than her smile. "You're remarkable," she says. "I haven't met a human worth collecting in a very long time." "I'm not a dog." "No," Makima agrees, finally stepping back, the string dissolving from her wrist like morning frost. "Not yet." She walks away, heels clicking on concrete, and Jolyne watches her go with her heart hammering against her ribs. The fence rattles. Jolyne doesn't look away from Makima's retreating form until long after she's disappeared through the facility doors. She's going to need more strings.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, well-controlled crossover scene that hits the brief: third person, present tense, roughly the requested length, Jolyne suspicious of Makima's sweetness, Makima intrigued by the Stand, escalating into a tense standoff. Strengths: The prose is clean and economical, with a strong opening hook (the silent walk, the fence rattles as a recurring motif). Jolyne's voice is well captured—foul-mouthed, defensive, sharp—and her famous quote is repurposed cleverly as a plot beat ("You're selling me a fantasy") rather than dropped in as decoration. Makima's menace is conveyed effectively through restraint: the too-perfect smile, the parting inmates, the pressure against Jolyne's mind. The moment where Jolyne is genuinely tempted by Makima's offer before rejecting it gives the confrontation emotional weight and avoids a flat heroic refusal. The "Not yet" closing line is a nicely chilling beat for Makima. Weaknesses: The scene is somewhat safe and talky—the "battle of wits" never escalates into real danger or consequence, and Makima retreats with uncharacteristic ease, deflating tension rather than raising it. Makima's dialogue occasionally over-explains her own nature ("They've all been so cooperative... You're different"), edging toward tell-don't-show, though the physical details (the silent approach, the eyes) mostly compensate. The middle section relies on familiar beats (temptation offer, refusal, threat) and the ending, while atmospheric, is predictable. Some imagery is stock ("like fish parting around a shark," "thin as spider silk and strong as steel"). Jolyne's monologue about her family is efficient but slightly expository. Overall: a polished, engaging character piece with authentic voices and good atmosphere, held back by a conventional structure and a resolution that arrives too comfortably. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 78.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7412 — Temporal Correspondence from a Future Self --- **Item #:** SCP-7412 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** All recovered notes designated SCP-7412-1 through -14 are stored in a locked evidence locker at Site-42. Researcher Maren Cole is no longer permitted to work alone. All work sessions are recorded. Psychological evaluations occur weekly. I remember when that last part felt excessive. --- It started on a Tuesday. Ordinary in every way a Tuesday at the Foundation can be ordinary. I was cataloguing anomalous objects recovered from a warehouse in Tucson—low-threat items, mostly reality-bending refuse—and I found a folded note tucked between two file folders on my desk. The handwriting was mine. I know this because I've seen my own handwriting thousands of times. The way I loop my G's. The slight leftward slant I've never been able to correct. But I had no memory of writing it. The note read: *"Don't submit the Tucson inventory. Not yet. Something in Box 7 isn't what the manifest says. You'll understand on the 19th."* I checked the date on my computer. It was the 12th. I told myself it was stress. I'd been pulling long hours. Maybe I wrote it during a dissociative episode and forgot. I submitted the inventory anyway, including Box 7, which contained a ceramic figurine that registered no anomalous properties. Nothing happened on the 19th. --- The second note appeared four days later, inside my coffee mug. Same handwriting. Different ink—darker, thicker, almost like it had been written with something that wasn't a pen at all. *"You submitted it. God, why didn't you listen? The figurine. It's not ceramic. It's not ceramic. On the 19th it wakes up and you can't see it because it doesn't want you to. Check the thermodynamic readings. Check them. You won't."* I checked the thermodynamic readings on the figurine. Standard. No fluctuations. No anomalous heat signatures. But the ink. Dr. Voss in Materials Analysis confirmed what I'd suspected. The ink contained trace elements of gallium, carbonite compounds not found in any commercial pen, and something she couldn't identify—a molecular structure that resembled ink but bonded to paper at a level she described as "almost cellular." "Like it grew into the page," she said. I didn't sleep that night. --- Note three came inside a locked drawer I'd checked an hour prior. *"The breach starts in Sector C. Don't go to Sector C. I went to Sector C. That's where it— no. No. The figurine is in Sector C now. I moved it. Did I move it? The manifest says Box 7 but the manifest is wrong. Everything in the manifest is wrong. They're going to tell you it's psychological. They're going to say I'm not real. But I'm you. I'm you in eleven days and I'm begging you."* Eleven days from when? I reported it this time. Dr. Hwang, my supervisor, pulled me from the Tucson project and scheduled a full psychological evaluation. I passed. No dissociative episodes. No history of mental illness. No evidence of memetic exposure. But the notes kept coming. --- Note seven was written on the back of a Foundation requisition form dated three weeks in the future. The form had my signature on it. I had not signed any such form. *"The walls in Observation Room 4 breathe at night. I know you don't believe me. I didn't believe me either. But they breathe and the figurine is alive and it's not from Tucson. It was never from Tucson. It came from inside. Inside what? Inside US. Inside the Foundation. It grew here. We grew it."* Note nine was just one sentence, repeated forty-seven times until the pen had torn through the paper: *"Don't trust the walls don't trust the walls don't trust the walls don't trust"* Note eleven contradicted everything. It said the figurine had been destroyed. It said the figurine had never existed. It said I had never existed, that Maren Cole was a name the entity had given itself to feel human, and that the notes were not warnings but memories bleeding backward through a timeline that was unraveling. The ink analysis on note eleven showed the same unidentified compound. But this time, there were also trace amounts of blood. Mine. Type O-negative, confirmed by DNA. --- The Foundation contained SCP-7412 by containing me. I was moved to a monitored room. No access to my office. No access to the Tucson files. No access to the figurine, which still registered as non-anomalous. And still the notes appeared. Note fourteen was on my pillow when I woke up. Two cameras watched me sleep. Neither showed anyone entering the room. Neither showed me moving. The note read: *"It's tomorrow now. I'm you. I'm still you. The breach happened. You just can't see it because you're inside it. The walls have always breathed. The figurine was always alive. You were always me."* Below that, in handwriting that was mine but shakier, smaller, like a child's: *"Please. Please believe me. Please."* --- The investigation is ongoing. Dr. Hwang believes SCP-7412 may be a localized temporal anomaly tied to the Tucson warehouse objects. Dr. Voss believes the ink compound suggests an external intelligence. The psychological team believes I may be a risk to myself. I don't know what I believe anymore. I keep thinking about the figurine. How ordinary it looked. How I held it in my hands and felt nothing. But last night, alone in my monitored room, I heard something. A sound like breathing. Slow. Wet. Coming from the walls. And for just a moment—just a fraction of a second—I could have sworn the ceramic figurine was sitting on my desk. But it wasn't. It couldn't have been. They told me it couldn't have been. I'm writing this down because I need to remember what's real. I need to remember the order of things. I need to trust that the walls are walls, that the figurine is ceramic, that I am who they say I am. But note fifteen is in my pocket right now, and I don't know how it got there. I haven't read it yet. I'm afraid it will be in my handwriting.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong pastiche of SCP Foundation format fiction, blending clinical containment-document conventions with a first-person researcher narrative in past tense, as instructed. The structural conceit—interspersed notes escalating from coherent warning to desperate incoherence—is executed effectively. The notes progress logically from specific, actionable warnings ("Don't submit the Tucson inventory") to contradictions of known reality ("the figurine had never existed... I had never existed"), fulfilling the prompt's requirements directly. The Foundation's dual-investigation angle (temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation) is present via Dr. Hwang's and Dr. Voss's competing theories and the psych evaluations, though it's somewhat compressed—more procedural detail would have strengthened that dimension. The researcher's struggle to trust their own perception is the piece's emotional core and is handled well, particularly in the ending's refusal to resolve ("I haven't read it yet"). Strengths: The ink analysis detail ("bonded to paper at a level she described as 'almost cellular'") is a good grounded-forensic touch. Note nine's repetition to physical destruction of the page is a vivid escalation. The final line is an effective cliffhanger that avoids false resolution. Prose is clean and controlled, mostly avoiding purple excess. The unreliability of the narrator is well-sustained—the hallucinated figurine moment is earned by prior setup. Weaknesses: The word count is roughly 1000, appropriate. The pacing in the middle section compresses too many notes into summary (notes 7, 9, 11 in quick succession), which slightly robs the middle of tension-building that individual scenes would provide. Some elements are familiar to the genre—the "it was inside us all along" reveal, breathing walls, and the containment-breach-that-is-perceptual are stock SCP/tropes, though competently handled. Dr. Hwang and Dr. Voss are functional rather than fleshed out. Dialogue is minimal but serviceable. The twist that the anomaly may be perceptual could be seen coming, but the piece wisely withholds confirmation. The tone is consistent—clinical sections read clinical, narrative sections read anxious and grounded. The gradual erosion of the narrator's certainty is believable. There are no unearned transformations; the researcher's psychological unraveling is incremental and plausible. # SCP-7842 **Item #:** SCP-7842 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Mobile Task Force Iota-12 ("Threshold Watch") is tasked with identifying and securing SCP-7842 instances worldwide. Discovered doors are to be locked, welded shut, and the surrounding building acquired as Foundation property under appropriate cover stories. No Foundation personnel below Level 4 clearance are permitted entry to SCP-7842-1. Personnel files matching current staff (see Addendum 7842-C) are classified at Level 5/7842. Investigation into O5 activities related to SCP-7842 is suspended pending Council review. **Description:** SCP-7842 is the collective designation for 37 identical doors discovered in abandoned or condemned structures across 19 countries as of 11/2024. Doors are constructed of an unidentified dark wood, measure 2.1m × 0.9m, and bear no hardware, markings, or manufacturer indicators. Notably, individual doors display varying degrees of weathering inconsistent with their host structures—several instances found in buildings less than 20 years old show advanced deterioration, carbon dating suggesting ages exceeding 600 years. SCP-7842-1 is the extradimensional space accessible through SCP-7842 doors. It consists of an apparently limitless archive of shelving, filing systems, and document storage extending beyond visual range in all directions. Architecture is internally inconsistent: corridors connect at non-Euclidean angles, rooms contain spatial anomalies, and sections appear to exist in different temporal states. Lighting is provided by an unidentifiable ambient source. Documents within SCP-7842-1 are written in multiple languages, including extinct and unidentified scripts. Translatable materials reference a global civilization designated "the Concordat" destroyed by an event described only as "Seventh-Breach Cascade" or "the Unmaking." No further specifics have been recovered. --- **Addendum 7842-A: Exploration Log 7842-1** *Exploration Team: Zeta-4 (four personnel)* *Entry Point: SCP-7842-7, abandoned textile factory, Manchester, UK* **[BEGIN LOG]** **Z4-1:** Door is open. Same dark wood. More weathered than the last one—surface is almost black with age. This building was condemned in 2019, but the door looks centuries older. **Z4-3:** Confirmed. Entering. *[Team enters SCP-7842-1. Standard corridor, shelving extending approximately 40m visible before darkness.]* **Z4-2:** Aisles 1 through 12 on the left are labeled. "Administrative Records," "Personnel," "Containment Protocols"—wait. "Containment Protocols"? **Z4-1:** Log everything. Move deeper. *[Team proceeds 200m. Corridors multiply. Temperature drops noticeably.]* **Z4-4:** Captain. Movement ahead. *[Distant figures observed approximately 60m ahead. Three humanoid entities wearing full-body suits resembling hazmat gear, matte gray with no visible seams or markings. Entities are removing shelves and documents, placing them into large containers that appear to fold into themselves.]* **Z4-1:** Approach slowly. *[Team advances 20m. Entities become aware of team presence. All three entities immediately cease activity, abandon containers, and flee deeper into the archive. Movement is rapid but not superhuman. Containers left behind dissolve within seconds.]* **Z4-3:** They're gone. The shelves they were clearing—empty now. But there are marks. Dust outlines where binders sat. **Z4-1:** What were they removing? **Z4-2:** Can't tell. Everything's gone. But there are discarded pages on the floor. Torn, like they were pulled from bindings quickly. *[Recovered fragment, translated from modern English:]* > *...Concordat Directive 7-Omega authorizes final transfer of remaining archival materials to Secondary Site. Primary sites no longer viable following [illegible]... Seventh-Breach Cascade has consumed [illegible]... all personnel records for Project SHEPHERD must be...* **Z4-4:** Captain. Over here. *[Team discovers a reading alcove. Desk, chair, lamp. On the desk: a leather binder, open.]* **Z4-1:** What is this? **Z4-2:** It's... Captain, this is a personnel file. Standard format. Photo, credentials, assignment history. **Z4-3:** Whose? **Z4-2:** Yours. Captain Elena Vasquez. Born 1981. Assigned to MTF Zeta-4 in 2019. **Z4-1:** That's correct. **Z4-2:** This document is dated 1847. The photograph is you. The signature is yours. *[Silence, 8 seconds.]* **Z4-1:** Continue searching the alcove. *[Additional files recovered. See Addendum 7842-C.]* **Z4-4:** Found something else. Visitor log. Recent entries. *[Excerpt:]* > *14/03/2024 — Visitor: [REDACTED], O5-3. Purpose: Review of Concordat-era personnel files. Duration: 4 hours, 12 minutes.* > > *02/06/2024 — Visitor: [REDACTED], O5-9. Purpose: Unspecified. Duration: 7 hours, 41 minutes.* > > *19/09/2024 — Visitor: [REDACTED], O5-3. Purpose: Document retrieval. Duration: 2 hours, 03 minutes.* **Z4-1:** O5 Council members have been here. Multiple times. Without authorization. Without anyone knowing. **Z4-2:** The log goes back further. Years. **Z4-3:** What have they been reading? **Z4-1:** Pack everything. We're leaving. Now. *[Team withdraws. Exit without incident.]* **[END LOG]** --- **Addendum 7842-B: Recovered Document Excerpt** *The following was found intact in a section of SCP-7842-1 approximately 3km from the entry point, in a room labeled "Concordat Central Command — Final Transmissions."* > *To any who find this archive:* > > *The Concordat existed to contain that which threatens humanity. We succeeded for four centuries. We failed because we believed our containment was eternal.* > > *The Seventh-Breach Cascade began with a single anomaly we believed was understood. It was not. By the time we recognized the cascade, seven containment sites had fallen simultaneously. We could not stop what followed.* > > *This archive is all that remains of our work. We have hidden it beyond the reach of what consumed us. If you have found these doors, then something of humanity survived. Perhaps you have built your own organization to do what we did.* > > *Be warned: the cascade does not end. It waits. It is patient. What we failed to contain is still uncontained.* > > *And it remembers us.* > > *— Final entry, Concordat Administrator [NAME REDACTED]* --- **Addendum 7842-C: Personnel Files** Recovered files match current Foundation personnel with 94% accuracy in biographical details, including photographs. Dates of record range from 1831 to 1856. Affected personnel include: - Captain Elena Vasquez (MTF Zeta-4) - Dr. Yuki Tanaka (Site-19 Research) - Agent Marcus Cole (MTF Iota-12) - Dr. Sarah Chen (Site-19 Research) - [34 additional personnel files recovered] All affected personnel have been placed under observation. None recall any connection to "the Concordat" or any existence prior to their known lives. Investigation into O5-3 and O5-9's unauthorized visits is ongoing. Both Council members have declined to comment. **Addendum 7842-D:** On 02/12/2024, SCP-7842-7 was found welded shut from the inside.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry executes the prompt's requirements with strong fidelity: identical unmarked doors, an architecturally impossible archive, a prior civilization ("the Concordat") destroyed by an unspecified containment failure ("Seventh-Breach Cascade"), personnel files matching current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-entity removal teams that flee when approached, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The document format is authentic to SCP conventions—containment procedures, description, addenda, exploration logs, redactions—and the final line ("found welded shut from the inside") is an effective, understated closing sting. Strengths: the exploration log is well-paced, using terse radio-speak dialogue and physical detail (dust outlines where binders sat, containers that fold into themselves) to build dread economically. The reveal of the captain's own personnel file dated 1847 is the strongest beat, and the 8-second silence is a nice touch of show-don't-tell. The recovered Concordat transmission balances menace and pathos without over-explaining. Weaknesses: the prose is functional rather than elegant; the archive's description leans on generic phrases ("beyond visual range in all directions," "unidentifiable ambient source"). The Concordat's final message flirts with cliché ("It is patient... it remembers us"), and the twist that current personnel have past-life analogues is a familiar SCP trope handled without much fresh angle. The hazmat entities are introduced and dropped without escalation. Dialogue is serviceable but flat—mostly procedural callouts with little individual voice distinguishing team members. The O5 thread is raised and left dangling, which works as mystery but also feels like the entry gesturing at depth it doesn't fully earn. Emotionally, the piece is engaging but not complex; dread is present, grief and wonder less so. Overall: a competent, professional SCP pastiche that fulfills every instruction, with a few genuinely effective moments, held back by safe, formulaic execution.
